Chapter 8 — Support Vector Machines

Chapter 7 ended with a curious fact: gradient descent on the logistic loss, run on separable data, drifts toward the separating hyperplane with the largest margin, and that hyperplane depends only on the few training examples that sit on the margin. This chapter starts from that hyperplane. We derive the support vector machine from the geometry of the margin, obtain its dual problem and see why the solution is sparse in the examples, extend it to data that cannot be separated with the hinge loss, solve it with a subgradient method and with the SMO algorithm, and measure what the margin buys in generalization.

8.1 Learning objectives¶

Chapters 3 and 6 gave two separate reasons to look for a large margin. Theorem 3.7 bounds the error of a linear classifier by the fraction of training points below a margin γ\gammaγ plus a term proportional to ∥w∥/γ\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert/\gamma∥w∥/γ, so that a classifier with a large margin and a small norm generalizes well whatever the dimension. Section 6.4.4 found that on separable data the logistic regression has no maximum-likelihood estimate and that the weights diverge, and Section 7.7.3 showed where the direction of the divergence leads. The support vector machine (SVM) turns this around: instead of waiting for an optimizer to find a large margin, it asks for the largest margin directly, as the solution of a convex optimization problem.

After working through the chapter you will be able to:

  1. define the geometric margin of a hyperplane and formulate the hard-margin SVM as the quadratic program “minimize 12∥w∥2\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^221​∥w∥2 subject to yi(w⊤xi+b)≥1y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ge 1yi​(w⊤xi​+b)≥1”;

  2. derive the dual problem and the KKT conditions, and use them to show that w\mathbf{w}w is a combination of the support vectors only, that the margin is 2/∥w∥2/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert2/∥w∥ and that ∥w∥2=∑iαi\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\alpha_i∥w∥2=∑i​αi​;

  3. solve a small SVM by hand, through the guess of the support set and the verification of the KKT conditions;

  4. extend the formulation to non-separable data with slack variables, show that it is the minimization of the hinge loss plus a ridge penalty with λ=1/(Cn)\lambda = 1/(Cn)λ=1/(Cn), and interpret the three kinds of examples (αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0, 0<αi<C0 < \alpha_i < C0<αi​<C, αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C);

  5. explain what the hinge loss estimates (the Bayes classifier itself, not the probabilities) and compare it with the logistic loss;

  6. prove the convergence rate of the subgradient method with the step 1/(λk)1/(\lambda k)1/(λk), derive the SMO update, and implement both from scratch;

  7. state and prove the leave-one-out bound err^LOO≤#SV/n\widehat{\mathrm{err}}_{\mathrm{LOO}}\le\#\mathrm{SV}/nerrLOO​≤#SV/n, evaluate the margin bound of Chapter 3 on a real data set and choose CCC with the protocols of Chapter 5;

  8. use SVMs in practice with scikit-learn (feature scaling, comparison with logistic regression, probabilities by Platt scaling, multiclass by one-vs-one and one-vs-rest), and see how the dual form leads to kernels (Chapter 9) and to support vector regression.

Prerequisites. Chapters 1 to 7. In particular the margin bound of Section 3.8.4, the cross-validation protocols and McNemar’s test of Chapter 5, regularized logistic regression and the meaning of CCC (Section 6.5), the dual form of ridge regression (Proposition 6.12), and the implicit bias of gradient descent (Section 7.7.3). Constrained optimization is used through Lagrange multipliers; every step is derived here.

A word about the data in this chapter

The experiments use real data sets, all shipped with scikit-learn: Iris (two petal measurements, for pictures in the plane), Breast Cancer (the main example: the stratified split of Chapters 6 and 7, with 426 training and 143 test patients, malignant =1= 1=1), Digits (multiclass) and Diabetes (regression). The only constructions that are not data are the five points of Worked example 8.1, small enough to be solved by hand, and the explicit-feature check of Section 8.8, which is a numerical identity. In this chapter the two classes are labeled yi∈{−1,+1}y_i \in \{-1, +1\}yi​∈{−1,+1}, as in Section 3.8.4, and the score of an example is f(x)=w⊤x+bf(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + bf(x)=w⊤x+b with the intercept bbb kept apart from w\mathbf{w}w (unlike Chapter 7, where it was one of the coordinates).

8.2 The hard-margin support vector machine¶

8.2.1 Margins and the largest-margin hyperplane¶

A linear classifier predicts sign⁡(w⊤x+b)\operatorname{sign}(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b)sign(w⊤x+b). The hyperplane H={x:w⊤x+b=0}H = \{\mathbf{x} : \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = 0\}H={x:w⊤x+b=0} separates the space in two half-spaces, and the size of the score of a point says how far from HHH it is.

Proposition 8.1 (distance to a hyperplane)

The distance from a point x\mathbf{x}x to the hyperplane HHH is ∣w⊤x+b∣/∥w∥\lvert\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\rvert/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∣w⊤x+b∣/∥w∥. Consequently, if yi(w⊤xi+b)≥1y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ge 1yi​(w⊤xi​+b)≥1 for all iii and equality holds for at least one example of each class, the two parallel hyperplanes w⊤x+b=±1\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = \pm 1w⊤x+b=±1 are at distance 2/∥w∥2/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert2/∥w∥ from each other, and no training point lies between them.

Proof

Let x0∈H\mathbf{x}_0 \in Hx0​∈H be the point of HHH closest to x\mathbf{x}x. The vector x−x0\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_0x−x0​ is orthogonal to HHH, hence parallel to w\mathbf{w}w: x=x0+t w/∥w∥\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_0 + t\,\mathbf{w}/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVertx=x0​+tw/∥w∥ for a real ttt, whose absolute value is the distance. Then w⊤x+b=w⊤x0+b+t∥w∥=t∥w∥\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_0 + b + t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = t\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVertw⊤x+b=w⊤x0​+b+t∥w∥=t∥w∥, so ∣t∣=∣w⊤x+b∣/∥w∥\lvert t\rvert = \lvert\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\rvert/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∣t∣=∣w⊤x+b∣/∥w∥. A point on w⊤x+b=1\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = 1w⊤x+b=1 is at distance 1/∥w∥1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert1/∥w∥ from HHH, and one on w⊤x+b=−1\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = -1w⊤x+b=−1 at the same distance on the other side. □\square□

Suppose the training set is linearly separable: some (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b) has yi(w⊤xi+b)>0y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) > 0yi​(w⊤xi​+b)>0 for all iii. There are then infinitely many separating hyperplanes (Figure 8.1), all with zero training error, and the question is which one to choose. The geometric margin of (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b) is the distance from HHH to the closest training point, γ=min⁡iyi(w⊤xi+b)/∥w∥\gamma = \min_i y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVertγ=mini​yi​(w⊤xi​+b)/∥w∥. The score does not change in sign if we multiply (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b) by a positive constant, and the margin is invariant under that change, so we may fix the scale by requiring that the closest points have score exactly ±1\pm 1±1. In this scale γ=1/∥w∥\gamma = 1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVertγ=1/∥w∥ (Proposition 8.1) and maximizing the margin is the same as minimizing ∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥:

 min⁡w,b 12∥w∥2subject toyi(w⊤xi+b) ≥ 1,i=1,…,n. (hard-margin primal)\boxed{\ \min_{\mathbf{w}, b}\ \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ \ge\ 1,\quad i = 1, \dots, n.\ } \tag{hard-margin primal} w,bmin​ 21​∥w∥2subject toyi​(w⊤xi​+b) ≥ 1,i=1,…,n. ​(hard-margin primal)
(1)

This is a convex quadratic program: a strictly convex objective in w\mathbf{w}w with nnn linear inequality constraints. It has a solution if and only if the data are separable, and then the solution w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ is unique (the objective is strictly convex in w\mathbf{w}w and the feasible set is convex). The reason for choosing this hyperplane is the margin bound of Theorem 3.7: with the constraints yif(xi)≥1y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)\ge 1yi​f(xi​)≥1 the first term of the bound (the fraction of points with margin below γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1) is zero, and the second term is proportional to ∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥, which is the quantity that the SVM minimizes. Among all the separating hyperplanes, it is the one with the smallest value of the bound.

The next two cells set up the data of this section. The first is Worked example 8.1, five points in the plane small enough to solve by hand. The second is the data of Figure 8.1(b): the petal length and width of the setosa and versicolor flowers of Iris (100 flowers, 50 in each class), a real separable problem in two dimensions.

Worked example 8.1 — a five-point SVM by hand¶

Take the negative points x1=(0,0)\mathbf{x}_1 = (0, 0)x1​=(0,0), x2=(2,0)\mathbf{x}_2 = (2, 0)x2​=(2,0) and the positive points x3=(1,2)\mathbf{x}_3 = (1, 2)x3​=(1,2), x4=(3,3)\mathbf{x}_4 = (3, 3)x4​=(3,3), x5=(0,4)\mathbf{x}_5 = (0, 4)x5​=(0,4). This data set is constructed, to be solved in closed form. Looking at the picture (Figure 8.1(a)), the closest points of the two classes are x3\mathbf{x}_3x3​ and the segment between x1\mathbf{x}_1x1​ and x2\mathbf{x}_2x2​: guess that the support vectors are x1,x2,x3\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{x}_3x1​,x2​,x3​, that is, that the constraints of these three points hold with equality and the others are slack. The equalities are

x1:−(b)=1⇒ b=−1,x2:−(2w1+b)=1⇒ 2w1=−b−1=0,  w1=0,x3:w1+2w2+b=1⇒ 2w2=2,  w2=1.\begin{aligned} \mathbf{x}_1:&\quad -(b) = 1 &&\Rightarrow\ b = -1,\\ \mathbf{x}_2:&\quad -(2w_1 + b) = 1 &&\Rightarrow\ 2w_1 = -b - 1 = 0,\ \ w_1 = 0,\\ \mathbf{x}_3:&\quad w_1 + 2w_2 + b = 1 &&\Rightarrow\ 2w_2 = 2,\ \ w_2 = 1. \end{aligned}x1​:x2​:x3​:​−(b)=1−(2w1​+b)=1w1​+2w2​+b=1​​⇒ b=−1,⇒ 2w1​=−b−1=0,  w1​=0,⇒ 2w2​=2,  w2​=1.​
(2)

So w=(0,1)\mathbf{w} = (0, 1)w=(0,1), b=−1b = -1b=−1, and the margin is 1/∥w∥=11/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 11/∥w∥=1 (the two margin hyperplanes, w2=0w_2 = 0w2​=0 and w2=2w_2 = 2w2​=2, are at distance 2). The guess is right if the other constraints hold: x4\mathbf{x}_4x4​ has score 3−1=2≥13 - 1 = 2 \ge 13−1=2≥1 and x5\mathbf{x}_5x5​ has 4−1=3≥14 - 1 = 3 \ge 14−1=3≥1. That the guess is the optimal solution is what the dual of the next section proves: there we shall find α=(14,14,12,0,0)\boldsymbol\alpha = (\tfrac14, \tfrac14, \tfrac12, 0, 0)α=(41​,41​,21​,0,0). The code below solves the problem numerically (scikit-learn’s SVC with a very large CCC is a hard-margin SVM when the data are separable) and also with a general-purpose optimizer applied directly to the primal.

X_we = np.array([[0, 0], [2, 0], [1, 2], [3, 3], [0, 4]], dtype=float)           # constructed example
y_we = np.array([-1, -1, 1, 1, 1], dtype=float)

hard_we = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-10).fit(X_we, y_we)
print("sklearn:      w =", hard_we.coef_.round(6).ravel(), " b =", hard_we.intercept_.round(6), " support vectors:", hard_we.support_ + 1)
print("alpha_i y_i for the support vectors:", hard_we.dual_coef_.round(6).ravel())

constraints = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda v, i=i: y_we[i] * (X_we[i] @ v[:2] + v[2]) - 1} for i in range(len(y_we))]
primal = minimize(lambda v: 0.5 * v[:2] @ v[:2], x0=np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1]), constraints=constraints, method="SLSQP",
                  options={"ftol": 1e-14, "maxiter": 500})
print("direct primal: w =", primal.x[:2].round(6), " b =", primal.x[2].round(6))
print("scores of the five points:", (X_we @ hard_we.coef_.ravel() + hard_we.intercept_).round(4))

8.2.2 The dual problem and the support vectors¶

The primal has d+1d + 1d+1 unknowns and nnn constraints. Attaching a multiplier αi≥0\alpha_i \ge 0αi​≥0 to each constraint gives the Lagrangian

L(w,b,α)=12∥w∥2−∑i=1nαi[yi(w⊤xi+b)−1],\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol\alpha) = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 - \sum_{i=1}^n \alpha_i\big[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) - 1\big],L(w,b,α)=21​∥w∥2−i=1∑n​αi​[yi​(w⊤xi​+b)−1],
(3)

and the derivation below shows how it leads to a different problem, in the nnn unknowns αi\alpha_iαi​, whose solution gives the one of the primal.

Theorem 8.2 (dual problem and KKT conditions of the hard-margin SVM)

Let the data be separable. The primal has a unique solution w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^, and there are multipliers α^i≥0\hat\alpha_i \ge 0α^i​≥0 that solve the dual problem

max⁡α  ∑i=1nαi−12∑i=1n∑j=1nαiαj yiyj xi⊤xjsubject toαi≥0,∑i=1nαiyi=0,\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\ \ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^n\alpha_i\alpha_j\,y_iy_j\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad \alpha_i\ge 0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iy_i = 0,αmax​  i=1∑n​αi​−21​i=1∑n​j=1∑n​αi​αj​yi​yj​xi⊤​xj​subject toαi​≥0,i=1∑n​αi​yi​=0,

with no gap between the primal and the dual optimal values. The solutions are linked by

w^=∑i=1nα^i yi xi,α^i [yi(w^⊤xi+b^)−1]=0  for every i(complementary slackness).\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_{i=1}^n\hat\alpha_i\,y_i\,\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \hat\alpha_i\,\big[y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) - 1\big] = 0\ \text{ for every } i\quad\text{(complementary slackness)}.w^=i=1∑n​α^i​yi​xi​,α^i​[yi​(w^⊤xi​+b^)−1]=0  for every i(complementary slackness).
(5)

Consequently: (i) only the examples on the margin (yi(w^⊤xi+b^)=1y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) = 1yi​(w^⊤xi​+b^)=1), the support vectors, can have α^i>0\hat\alpha_i > 0α^i​>0, and w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ is a combination of them alone; (ii) ∥w^∥2=∑iα^i\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\hat\alpha_i∥w^∥2=∑i​α^i​, so the margin is 1/∑iα^i1/\sqrt{\sum_i\hat\alpha_i}1/∑i​α^i​​; (iii) the data enter the dual only through the inner products xi⊤xj\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jxi⊤​xj​; (iv) the prediction is sign⁡(∑iα^iyi xi⊤x+b^)\operatorname{sign}\big(\sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x} + \hat b\big)sign(∑i​α^i​yi​xi⊤​x+b^), and the intercept is obtained from any support vector, b^=yk−w^⊤xk\hat b = y_k - \hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_kb^=yk​−w^⊤xk​.

The Lagrangian is convex and differentiable in (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b), and it is bounded below only if the derivative in bbb vanishes. which is the dual objective. No gap. The primal is a convex problem with affine constraints, which is feasible when the data are separable; for such problems strong duality holds (the refined Slater condition), so the maximum of the dual equals the minimum of the primal and a dual solution α^\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}α^ exists. At the optimum the minimizer of L(⋅,⋅,α^)\mathcal{L}(\cdot, \cdot, \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha})L(⋅,⋅,α^) is the primal solution, which gives w^=∑iα^iyixi\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw^=∑i​α^i​yi​xi​, and the equality of the optimal values gives complementary slackness: 12∥w^∥2=L(w^,b^,α^)=12∥w^∥2−∑iα^i[ yi(w^⊤xi+b^)−1]\tfrac12\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 = \mathcal{L}(\hat{\mathbf{w}}, \hat b, \hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}) = \tfrac12\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 - \sum_i\hat\alpha_i[\,y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b) - 1]21​∥w^∥2=L(w^,b^,α^)=21​∥w^∥2−∑i​α^i​[yi​(w^⊤xi​+b^)−1], a sum of non-negative terms that must therefore all vanish. Consequences. (i) is complementary slackness. For (ii), multiply w^=∑iα^iyixi\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw^=∑i​α^i​yi​xi​ by w^⊤\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\topw^⊤: ∥w^∥2=∑iα^i yiw^⊤xi=∑iα^i(1−yib^)\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\hat\alpha_i\,y_i\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i = \sum_i\hat\alpha_i(1 - y_i\hat b)∥w^∥2=∑i​α^i​yi​w^⊤xi​=∑i​α^i​(1−yi​b^), using yiw^⊤xi=1−yib^y_i\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i = 1 - y_i\hat byi​w^⊤xi​=1−yi​b^ whenever α^i>0\hat\alpha_i > 0α^i​>0, and ∑iα^iyi=0\sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​α^i​yi​=0 kills the term in b^\hat bb^. (iii) and (iv) are read off the formulas. The primal solution is unique because the objective is strictly convex in w\mathbf{w}w; b^\hat bb^ is then determined by any support vector, and there is one of each class because ∑iα^iyi=0\sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​α^i​yi​=0 with some α^i>0\hat\alpha_i > 0α^i​>0 forces both signs to appear. □\square□

Statement (i) is the sparsity of the SVM: after training, the examples with α^i=0\hat\alpha_i = 0α^i​=0 could be deleted without changing the classifier. In Worked example 8.1 the dual confirms the guess. Writing w=∑iαiyixi\mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw=∑i​αi​yi​xi​ with the three support vectors, (0,1)=−α1(0,0)−α2(2,0)+α3(1,2)=(α3−2α2, 2α3)(0, 1) = -\alpha_1(0, 0) - \alpha_2(2, 0) + \alpha_3(1, 2) = (\alpha_3 - 2\alpha_2,\ 2\alpha_3)(0,1)=−α1​(0,0)−α2​(2,0)+α3​(1,2)=(α3​−2α2​, 2α3​), so α3=12\alpha_3 = \tfrac12α3​=21​ and α2=14\alpha_2 = \tfrac14α2​=41​; the constraint ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0 gives α1=α3−α2=14\alpha_1 = \alpha_3 - \alpha_2 = \tfrac14α1​=α3​−α2​=41​; and (ii) holds: ∥w∥2=1=14+14+12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = 1 = \tfrac14 + \tfrac14 + \tfrac12∥w∥2=1=41​+41​+21​. All the αi\alpha_iαi​ are non-negative and α4=α5=0\alpha_4 = \alpha_5 = 0α4​=α5​=0 for the points off the margin, so (α,w,b)(\boldsymbol\alpha, \mathbf{w}, b)(α,w,b) satisfies all the KKT conditions and, by the theorem, is optimal.

def check_dual(model, X, y):
    """Check the consequences of Theorem 8.2 for a fitted hard-margin linear SVC (y in {-1, +1}),
    comparing with the solution of the primal problem obtained by a general-purpose optimizer."""
    sv = model.support_
    alpha_y = model.dual_coef_.ravel()                       # alpha_i * y_i for the support vectors
    w_dual = alpha_y @ X[sv]                                 # w = sum_i alpha_i y_i x_i
    cons = [{"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda v, i=i: y[i] * (X[i] @ v[:-1] + v[-1]) - 1} for i in range(len(y))]
    start = np.r_[model.coef_.ravel() * 1.05, model.intercept_]
    primal_sol = minimize(lambda v: 0.5 * v[:-1] @ v[:-1], start, constraints=cons, method="SLSQP", options={"ftol": 1e-14, "maxiter": 1000}).x
    scores = y * model.decision_function(X)
    print(f"  support vectors: {len(sv)} of {len(y)};  largest |w_primal - sum alpha_i y_i x_i| = {np.abs(primal_sol[:-1] - w_dual).max():.1e}")
    print(f"  sum alpha_i y_i = {alpha_y.sum():.1e};  sum alpha_i = {np.abs(alpha_y).sum():.6f};  ||w||^2 = {primal_sol[:-1] @ primal_sol[:-1]:.6f}")
    print(f"  smallest score y_i f(x_i) over the non-support vectors: {np.delete(scores, sv).min():.4f}  (> 1);  scores of the support vectors: "
          f"{scores[sv].min():.4f} to {scores[sv].max():.4f}  (= 1)")


print("Worked example 8.1:")
check_dual(hard_we, X_we, y_we)

8.2.3 Many separators, one margin: two pictures¶

Figure 8.1 shows the two problems. In panel (a) the five points of the worked example, the maximum-margin line and the margin hyperplanes. In panel (b), 100 real flowers (setosa and versicolor, petal length and width in centimeters) and the SVM line, drawn with two other separating lines found by the perceptron algorithm from different random orderings of the data: they have zero training error as well, and almost nothing keeps them away from the points.

mask_sv = iris.target < 2                                           # setosa (0) and versicolor (1)
X_ir = iris.data[mask_sv][:, 2:4]                                   # petal length and petal width, in cm
y_ir = 2.0 * iris.target[mask_sv] - 1                               # -1 = setosa, +1 = versicolor
hard_ir = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-10).fit(X_ir, y_ir)
print("Iris setosa/versicolor, hard margin:")
print(f"  w = {hard_ir.coef_.ravel().round(4)}, b = {hard_ir.intercept_[0]:.4f}, margin width 2/||w|| = {2 / np.linalg.norm(hard_ir.coef_):.4f} cm, "
      f"support vectors: examples {hard_ir.support_} (indices from 0)")
check_dual(hard_ir, X_ir, y_ir)
perceptrons = [Perceptron(random_state=s_, max_iter=1000, tol=None, eta0=1.0).fit(X_ir, y_ir) for s_ in (1, 3)]

def figure_8_1():
    def draw_line(ax, w, b, level, **kw):
        xs = np.array(ax.get_xlim())
        if abs(w[1]) > 1e-12:
            ax.plot(xs, (level - b - w[0] * xs) / w[1], **kw)
        else:
            ax.axvline((level - b) / w[0], **kw)

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.4, 4.3))
    ax = axes[0]
    ax.set_xlim(-1, 4.2), ax.set_ylim(-1, 5)

    ax.scatter(*X_we[y_we == 1].T, s=70, color=BLUE, marker="o", label="$y = +1$")
    ax.scatter(*X_we[hard_we.support_].T, s=260, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=1.6)
    w_, b_ = hard_we.coef_.ravel(), hard_we.intercept_[0]
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 0, color="k", lw=2)
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 1, color="k", lw=1.2, ls="--")
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, -1, color="k", lw=1.2, ls="--")
    for i, (px, py) in enumerate(X_we):
        ax.annotate(f"$x_{i + 1}$", (px, py), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(8, 6), fontsize=10)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(2.9, 0.0 + 1.0), xytext=(2.9, 0.0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="0.3"))
    ax.text(3.0, 0.45, "margin 1", fontsize=9, color="0.3")
    ax.set(xlabel="$x_1$", ylabel="$x_2$", title="(a) Worked example 8.1: three support vectors")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", fontsize=9)

    ax = axes[1]
    ax.set_xlim(0.5, 5.3), ax.set_ylim(-0.1, 2.0)

    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, 1, color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
    draw_line(ax, w_, b_, -1, color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.plot([], [], color="0.55", ls=":", label="two perceptron lines")

Two support vectors, one of each class, determine the line in panel (b), and w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ is a combination of them only: the other 98 flowers could be removed from the data set without changing the classifier. The numbers above verify the statements of Theorem 8.2 on this real problem: the vector w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^ found by minimizing the primal with a general-purpose optimizer equals ∑iαiyixi\sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_i∑i​αi​yi​xi​ computed from the dual coefficients of the solver of scikit-learn, ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0, and ∥w∥2=∑iαi\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\alpha_i∥w∥2=∑i​αi​. The support vectors are the two flowers closest to the other class; the width of the empty strip between the classes is 1.30 cm.

How this relates to Section 7.7.3

Section 7.7.3 computed the same hard-margin direction on the standardized petal measurements by running gradient descent for 106 steps, and found that its two active examples were the examples with indices 43 and 98 (counting from 0, as Python does). The two computations are not identical, for two reasons that are worth knowing. First, there the intercept was one of the coordinates of w\mathbf{w}w and was penalized (∥w^∥\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert∥w^∥ included it), while the SVM of this chapter leaves bbb out of the norm: this is also what makes the dual constraint ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0 appear. Second, the standardization changes the geometry of the plane. On the standardized data the two solutions differ by an angle of about 4∘4^\circ4∘ in the space of (b,w)(b, \mathbf{w})(b,w), with margins 0.646 (intercept penalized) and 0.658 (intercept free), and the same two support vectors; in the original units the support vectors are the examples 44 and 98. The maximum-margin classifier is not invariant to the scaling of the features (Section 8.7.1).

Z_ir = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_ir)
A_ir = np.c_[np.ones(len(y_ir)), Z_ir]
as_in_ch7 = LinearSVC(C=1e6, loss="hinge", fit_intercept=False, dual=True, max_iter=5_000_000, tol=1e-10).fit(A_ir, y_ir)      # intercept inside the norm
free_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-10).fit(Z_ir, y_ir)                                                              # intercept outside the norm
v1 = as_in_ch7.coef_.ravel()
v2 = np.r_[free_b.intercept_, free_b.coef_.ravel()]
print(f"intercept penalized (Chapter 7):  (b, w) = {v1.round(4)}, margin {1 / np.linalg.norm(v1):.4f}, active examples {np.flatnonzero(np.abs(y_ir * (A_ir @ v1) - 1) < 1e-5)}")
print(f"intercept free (this chapter):    (b, w) = {v2.round(4)}, margin {1 / np.linalg.norm(free_b.coef_):.4f}, support vectors {free_b.support_}")
print(f"angle between the two directions: {np.degrees(np.arccos(v1 @ v2 / np.linalg.norm(v1) / np.linalg.norm(v2))):.1f} degrees")

8.3 Data that cannot be separated: the soft margin¶

8.3.1 Slack variables and the hinge loss¶

Real data are rarely separable, and even when they are, as the Breast Cancer training set of Section 6.4.4, a hyperplane squeezed between the classes with a tiny margin can be a poor classifier (Exercise 7.10 and its solution showed it: the limit of gradient descent, the hard-margin classifier, has a lower test accuracy than the early-stopped iterates). The remedy is to allow some constraints to be violated, at a price. Introduce a slack variable ξi≥0\xi_i \ge 0ξi​≥0 for every example, which measures by how much the constraint of example iii is violated, and penalize their sum:

 min⁡w,b,ξ  12∥w∥2+C∑i=1nξisubject toyi(w⊤xi+b) ≥ 1−ξi,ξi≥0. (soft-margin primal)\boxed{\ \min_{\mathbf{w}, b, \boldsymbol\xi}\ \ \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ \ge\ 1 - \xi_i,\quad \xi_i\ge 0.\ } \tag{soft-margin primal} w,b,ξmin​  21​∥w∥2+Ci=1∑n​ξi​subject toyi​(w⊤xi​+b) ≥ 1−ξi​,ξi​≥0. ​(soft-margin primal)
(7)

The constant C>0C > 0C>0 sets the price of a violation: a large CCC approaches the hard-margin problem, a small CCC tolerates many violations in exchange for a wider margin. An example with ξi=0\xi_i = 0ξi​=0 is on the right side of its margin hyperplane; with 0<ξi≤10 < \xi_i \le 10<ξi​≤1 it is inside the strip but still correctly classified; with ξi>1\xi_i > 1ξi​>1 it is misclassified. For fixed (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b) the smallest feasible slack is the amount by which the constraint fails, ξi=max⁡{0, 1−yi(w⊤xi+b)}\xi_i = \max\{0,\ 1 - y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\}ξi​=max{0, 1−yi​(w⊤xi​+b)}, and substituting it gives an unconstrained problem.

Proposition 8.3 (the soft-margin SVM is regularized hinge-loss minimization)

Define the hinge loss of a margin m=y f(x)m = y\,f(\mathbf{x})m=yf(x) as ℓhinge(m)=max⁡{0, 1−m}\ell_{\text{hinge}}(m) = \max\{0,\ 1 - m\}ℓhinge​(m)=max{0, 1−m}. The soft-margin problem is equivalent to

min⁡w,b  1n∑i=1nℓhinge(yi(w⊤xi+b))+λ2∥w∥2, λ=1C n \min_{\mathbf{w}, b}\ \ \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_{\text{hinge}}\big(y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\big) + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2, \qquad \boxed{\ \lambda = \frac{1}{C\,n}\ }w,bmin​  n1​i=1∑n​ℓhinge​(yi​(w⊤xi​+b))+2λ​∥w∥2, λ=Cn1​ ​
(8)

in the sense that both have the same minimizers (the objective of the first is CnCnCn times the objective of the second).

Proof. For fixed (w,b)(\mathbf{w}, b)(w,b) the slacks enter the objective of the primal with a positive coefficient and are constrained from below by ξi≥0\xi_i\ge 0ξi​≥0 and ξi≥1−yif(xi)\xi_i\ge 1 - y_if(\mathbf{x}_i)ξi​≥1−yi​f(xi​), so the minimum over ξ\boldsymbol\xiξ is attained at ξi=max⁡{0,1−yif(xi)}\xi_i = \max\{0, 1 - y_if(\mathbf{x}_i)\}ξi​=max{0,1−yi​f(xi​)} and the objective becomes 12∥w∥2+C∑iℓhinge(mi)\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\ell_{\text{hinge}}(m_i)21​∥w∥2+C∑i​ℓhinge​(mi​). Dividing by CnCnCn gives the second form. □\square□

This is the same relation as in Section 6.5.1 (λ=1/(Cn)\lambda = 1/(Cn)λ=1/(Cn)), and it makes the point of the chapter in one line: the SVM is a regularized linear classifier, exactly like the ridge-penalized logistic regression, with the hinge loss in place of the logistic loss. The two losses are compared in Section 8.4. Everything that Chapter 6 said about CCC holds here: small CCC is strong regularization, a wide margin and a rigid model; large CCC is weak regularization, a narrow margin and a flexible model; and CCC must be chosen with the protocols of Chapter 5.

8.3.2 The dual problem and the three kinds of examples¶

The dual of the soft-margin problem differs from that of Theorem 8.2 in a single place: the multipliers are bounded above by CCC.

Theorem 8.4 (dual problem and KKT conditions of the soft-margin SVM)

The soft-margin primal has a solution and the dual problem

max⁡α  ∑i=1nαi−12∑i,jαiαj yiyj xi⊤xjsubject to0≤αi≤C,∑i=1nαiyi=0\max_{\boldsymbol\alpha}\ \ \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\,y_iy_j\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j \qquad\text{subject to}\qquad 0\le\alpha_i\le C,\quad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iy_i = 0αmax​  i=1∑n​αi​−21​i,j∑​αi​αj​yi​yj​xi⊤​xj​subject to0≤αi​≤C,i=1∑n​αi​yi​=0
(9)

has the same optimal value. A primal solution is w^=∑iα^iyixi\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_i\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw^=∑i​α^i​yi​xi​, and with the margins mi=yi(w^⊤xi+b^)m_i = y_i(\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat b)mi​=yi​(w^⊤xi​+b^) the optimality conditions are

α^i=0 ⇒ mi≥1,0<α^i<C ⇒ mi=1,α^i=C ⇒ mi≤1,\hat\alpha_i = 0\ \Rightarrow\ m_i\ge 1, \qquad 0 < \hat\alpha_i < C\ \Rightarrow\ m_i = 1, \qquad \hat\alpha_i = C\ \Rightarrow\ m_i\le 1,α^i​=0 ⇒ mi​≥1,0<α^i​<C ⇒ mi​=1,α^i​=C ⇒ mi​≤1,
(10)

and these implications are also sufficient. The examples are thus of three kinds: those beyond the margin (αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0, which do not enter w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^), those exactly on the margin (0<αi<C0 < \alpha_i < C0<αi​<C, the free support vectors), and those on or inside the margin or misclassified (αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C, the bounded support vectors, with slack ξi=1−mi≥0\xi_i = 1 - m_i \ge 0ξi​=1−mi​≥0). The intercept is obtained from the free support vectors, b^=yk−w^⊤xk\hat b = y_k - \hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_kb^=yk​−w^⊤xk​ for any free kkk.

Proof

Attach multipliers αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0 to the constraints yif(xi)−1+ξi≥0y_if(\mathbf{x}_i) - 1 + \xi_i\ge 0yi​f(xi​)−1+ξi​≥0 and μi≥0\mu_i\ge 0μi​≥0 to ξi≥0\xi_i\ge 0ξi​≥0:

L=12∥w∥2+C∑iξi−∑iαi[yi(w⊤xi+b)−1+ξi]−∑iμiξi.\mathcal{L} = \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i - \sum_i\alpha_i\big[y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b) - 1 + \xi_i\big] - \sum_i\mu_i\xi_i .L=21​∥w∥2+Ci∑​ξi​−i∑​αi​[yi​(w⊤xi​+b)−1+ξi​]−i∑​μi​ξi​.
(11)

The derivatives with respect to w\mathbf{w}w and bbb give, as before, w=∑iαiyixi\mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw=∑i​αi​yi​xi​ and ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0. The derivative with respect to ξi\xi_iξi​ is C−αi−μi=0C - \alpha_i - \mu_i = 0C−αi​−μi​=0, and since μi≥0\mu_i\ge 0μi​≥0 this means αi≤C\alpha_i\le Cαi​≤C (and μi=C−αi\mu_i = C - \alpha_iμi​=C−αi​). Substituting, the terms in ξi\xi_iξi​ cancel exactly (Cξi−αiξi−μiξi=0C\xi_i - \alpha_i\xi_i - \mu_i\xi_i = 0Cξi​−αi​ξi​−μi​ξi​=0) and we obtain the same dual function as in Theorem 8.2, now with the box constraint 0≤αi≤C0\le\alpha_i\le C0≤αi​≤C. The primal is a convex quadratic program with affine constraints and is feasible (take w=0\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}w=0, b=0b = 0b=0, ξi=1\xi_i = 1ξi​=1), so strong duality holds and the complementary slackness conditions are αi[ yif(xi)−1+ξi]=0\alpha_i[\,y_if(\mathbf{x}_i) - 1 + \xi_i] = 0αi​[yi​f(xi​)−1+ξi​]=0 and μiξi=(C−αi)ξi=0\mu_i\xi_i = (C - \alpha_i)\xi_i = 0μi​ξi​=(C−αi​)ξi​=0. If αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0 then μi=C>0\mu_i = C > 0μi​=C>0, so ξi=0\xi_i = 0ξi​=0 and the constraint gives mi≥1m_i\ge 1mi​≥1. If 0<αi<C0 < \alpha_i < C0<αi​<C then μi>0\mu_i > 0μi​>0 forces ξi=0\xi_i = 0ξi​=0, and αi>0\alpha_i > 0αi​>0 forces the constraint to be active: mi=1m_i = 1mi​=1. If αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C then the constraint is active, mi=1−ξi≤1m_i = 1 - \xi_i\le 1mi​=1−ξi​≤1. The sufficiency is the converse of the argument. □\square□

For C→∞C\to\inftyC→∞ the box constraint disappears and the dual becomes the dual of Theorem 8.2. When the data are separable the limit is reached at a finite CCC: if C0C_0C0​ is the largest multiplier of the hard-margin solution, every C≥C0C\ge C_0C≥C0​ gives exactly the same classifier (Exercise 8.4); below C0C_0C0​ the box constraint becomes active and the solution changes. The cells below show the soft margin on two real problems. The first is the two Iris species that overlap, versicolor and virginica (petal length and width in centimeters), where no hyperplane separates the classes.

mask_vv = iris.target > 0                                                # versicolor (1) and virginica (2)
X_vv = iris.data[mask_vv][:, 2:4]
y_vv = 2.0 * (iris.target[mask_vv] - 1) - 1                              # -1 = versicolor, +1 = virginica

rows, models_vv = [], {}
for C in [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100]:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-8).fit(X_vv, y_vv)
    models_vv[C] = m_
    alpha_ = np.abs(m_.dual_coef_.ravel())
    margins_ = y_vv * m_.decision_function(X_vv)
    rows.append({"C": C, "margin width 2/||w||": 2 / np.linalg.norm(m_.coef_), "support vectors": len(m_.support_),
                 "alpha = C": int(np.sum(alpha_ >= C - 1e-8)), "0 < alpha < C": int(np.sum(alpha_ < C - 1e-8)),
                 "margin violators": int(np.sum(margins_ < 1 - 1e-6)), "training errors": int(np.sum(margins_ <= 0))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))

    for ax, C in zip(axes, [0.01, 1, 100]):
        m_ = models_vv[C]
        w_, b_ = m_.coef_.ravel(), m_.intercept_[0]
        ax.scatter(*X_vv[y_vv == -1].T, s=24, color=VERMILION, marker="s", label="versicolor")
        ax.scatter(*X_vv[y_vv == 1].T, s=24, color=BLUE, marker="o", label="virginica")
        ax.scatter(*X_vv[m_.support_].T, s=120, facecolors="none", edgecolors="k", linewidths=1.0)
        ax.plot(xs, (-b_ - w_[0] * xs) / w_[1], color="k", lw=2)
        for level in (1, -1):
            ax.plot(xs, (level - b_ - w_[0] * xs) / w_[1], color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
        ax.set(xlim=(2.9, 7.1), ylim=(0.9, 2.65), xlabel="petal length (cm)",
               title=f"$C = {C:g}$: {len(m_.support_)} support vectors")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("petal width (cm)")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_2()

The progression is the one of Chapter 6. With a small CCC the margin is wide, nearly all the examples are inside it (they are support vectors with αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C) and the line is determined by the bulk of the data. With a large CCC the margin shrinks around a few examples near the boundary, the number of support vectors falls, and the line follows the overlap region more closely. The support vectors are not only the examples that are “hard”, but all those that are on or beyond the wrong side of their margin: for a small CCC they are the majority. The number of support vectors is a measure of the complexity of the solution, as we shall see in Section 8.6.

The second problem is the Breast Cancer training set, standardized, with C=1C = 1C=1 (the value that Section 6.5 selected for the logistic regression). The cell checks the conditions of Theorem 8.4, computes the primal objective 12∥w∥2+C∑iξi\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i21​∥w∥2+C∑i​ξi​ and the dual objective ∑iαi−12∥w∥2\sum_i\alpha_i - \tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2∑i​αi​−21​∥w∥2 from the solution of the solver, and shows what happens at the transition to the hard margin.

bc = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
Xb = bc.data.to_numpy()
yb = (1 - bc.target).to_numpy().astype(int)                              # malignant = 1, as in Chapters 6 and 7
Xb_tr, Xb_te, yb_tr, yb_te = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=yb)
scaler_b = StandardScaler().fit(Xb_tr)
Zb, Zb_te = scaler_b.transform(Xb_tr), scaler_b.transform(Xb_te)
sb, sb_te = 2.0 * yb_tr - 1, 2.0 * yb_te - 1                             # labels in {-1, +1}
n_b = len(sb)
print(f"Breast Cancer: {n_b} training patients, {Zb.shape[1]} features (standardized), {len(sb_te)} test patients; malignant = +1")


def dual_variables(model, n):
    alpha = np.zeros(n)
    alpha[model.support_] = np.abs(model.dual_coef_.ravel())
    return alpha


C_b = 1.0
svm_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C_b, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
alpha_b = dual_variables(svm_b, n_b)
m_b = sb * svm_b.decision_function(Zb)                                   # margins y_i f(x_i)
w_b = svm_b.coef_.ravel()
kinds = {"alpha = 0 (beyond the margin)": alpha_b <= 1e-9,
         "0 < alpha < C (on the margin)": (alpha_b > 1e-9) & (alpha_b < C_b - 1e-6),
         "alpha = C (inside, or misclassified)": alpha_b >= C_b - 1e-6}
rows = [{"kind": k, "examples": int(v.sum()), "smallest margin": m_b[v].min(), "largest margin": m_b[v].max(), "misclassified": int((m_b[v] <= 0).sum())}
        for k, v in kinds.items()]
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
slack = np.maximum(0, 1 - m_b)
primal_value = 0.5 * w_b @ w_b + C_b * slack.sum()
dual_value = alpha_b.sum() - 0.5 * w_b @ w_b
print(f"primal objective {primal_value:.6f}, dual objective {dual_value:.6f}; sum of alpha_i y_i = {alpha_b @ sb:.1e}; "
      f"test accuracy {np.mean(np.sign(svm_b.decision_function(Zb_te)) == sb_te):.4f}")

hard_b = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
C0 = np.abs(hard_b.dual_coef_).max()
print(f"hard margin: {len(hard_b.support_)} support vectors, ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(hard_b.coef_):.3f}, largest multiplier C0 = {C0:.2f}")
for factor in [0.25, 0.5, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 10]:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=factor * C0, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
    diff = np.linalg.norm(m_.coef_ - hard_b.coef_) / np.linalg.norm(hard_b.coef_)
    print(f"  C = {factor:>4} * C0 = {factor * C0:7.2f}: ||w|| = {np.linalg.norm(m_.coef_):7.3f}, relative distance from the hard-margin w = {diff:.1e}")

The 426 patients fall in the three kinds of Theorem 8.4 exactly as stated: 390 are beyond the margin (αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0; the smallest margin among them is 1.018 and the largest 31.5), 20 are exactly on it (0<αi<C0 < \alpha_i < C0<αi​<C; all with margin 1.0000), and 16 have αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C, with margins from -3.10 to 0.87, four of them misclassified. So 36 of the 426 examples (8.5%8.5\%8.5%) determine w^\hat{\mathbf{w}}w^, and 390 could be deleted without changing the classifier. The primal and dual objectives agree (19.0303 and 19.0303, up to the tolerance of the solver) and ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0. The test accuracy is 0.958 (6 errors among 143 patients). The last lines show the transition to the hard margin: its solution has 24 support vectors and ∥w^∥=28.4\lVert\hat{\mathbf{w}}\rVert = 28.4∥w^∥=28.4, the value that appeared in Exercise 7.10 (there the intercept was part of the norm), and its largest multiplier is C0=125C_0 = 125C0​=125. For every C≥C0C\ge C_0C≥C0​ the soft-margin solution is exactly the hard-margin one (relative distance 10-11 or zero), while at 0.9 C00.9\,C_00.9C0​ it is already 8%8\%8% away and at C0/4C_0/4C0​/4, 59%59\%59% away, with a norm of 13.6. The value C=1C = 1C=1 that works well in practice is two orders of magnitude below C0C_0C0​ and has ∥w∥=2.7\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert = 2.7∥w∥=2.7: the hard margin is the far end of a path, not the typical SVM.

8.4 The hinge loss, and what it estimates¶

8.4.1 Four losses of the margin¶

All the classifiers of Chapters 6 to 8 minimize an average of a loss of the margin m=y f(x)m = y\,f(\mathbf{x})m=yf(x) plus a penalty, and differ only in the loss. Figure 8.4 draws four of them as functions of mmm: the 0–1 loss I[m≤0]\mathbb{I}[m\le 0]I[m≤0] that we would like to minimize but cannot (it is not convex, nor continuous), the hinge loss max⁡{0,1−m}\max\{0, 1 - m\}max{0,1−m} of this chapter, its square max⁡{0,1−m}2\max\{0, 1 - m\}^2max{0,1−m}2 (the loss of LinearSVC by default, which is differentiable), and the logistic loss log⁡2(1+e−m)\log_2(1 + e^{-m})log2​(1+e−m) of Chapter 6 (divided by ln⁡2\ln 2ln2 so that it passes through the point (0,1)(0, 1)(0,1) like the others).

# Figure 8.4 — four losses as functions of the margin
def figure_8_4():
    m = np.linspace(-2.2, 2.2, 600)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
    ax.plot(m, (m <= 0).astype(float), color="k", lw=2, label="0–1 loss")
    ax.plot(m, np.maximum(0, 1 - m), color=BLUE, lw=2.2, label="hinge loss")
    ax.plot(m, np.maximum(0, 1 - m) ** 2, color=ORANGE, lw=2.2, ls="--", label="squared hinge loss")
    ax.plot(m, np.log2(1 + np.exp(-m)), color=VERMILION, lw=2.2, ls="-.", label=r"logistic loss, $\log_2(1 + e^{-m})$")
    ax.axvline(1, color="0.6", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"margin $m = y\,f(\mathbf{x})$", ylabel="loss", xlim=(-2.2, 2.2), ylim=(-0.05, 3.3), title="Surrogates of the 0–1 loss")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_4()

The hinge, the squared hinge and the logistic loss are convex upper bounds of the 0–1 loss, which makes them tractable surrogates (the hinge loss is the one that appears in the margin bound of Section 3.8.4 through the ramp loss φγ\varphi_\gammaφγ​, which it dominates). The difference that matters is at the right of the plot: the hinge loss is exactly zero for m≥1m\ge 1m≥1, so an example that is well classified with a margin of at least one has no influence on the solution (it has αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0), while the logistic loss is positive for every margin and every example keeps pulling on the weights, ever more weakly. This is the origin of the sparsity of the SVM. To compare the two precisely, return to the stationarity condition of the regularized logistic regression of Section 6.5, written in the scikit-learn parametrization where the objective is 12∥w∥2+C∑ilog⁡(1+e−mi)\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\log(1 + e^{-m_i})21​∥w∥2+C∑i​log(1+e−mi​). Setting the gradient in w\mathbf{w}w and in bbb to zero gives

w=∑i=1nαi yi xi,∑i=1nαiyi=0, αilogistic=C σ(−mi) \mathbf{w} = \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_i\,y_i\,\mathbf{x}_i, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^n\alpha_iy_i = 0, \qquad \boxed{\ \alpha_i^{\text{logistic}} = C\,\sigma(-m_i)\ }w=i=1∑n​αi​yi​xi​,i=1∑n​αi​yi​=0, αilogistic​=Cσ(−mi​) ​
(12)

with σ\sigmaσ the sigmoid. The logistic regression has the same representation as the SVM, as a combination of the training examples with weights αi∈(0,C)\alpha_i\in(0, C)αi​∈(0,C) and ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0; the difference is only the rule that gives the weights. For the hinge loss the rule is αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C if mi<1m_i < 1mi​<1, αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0 if mi>1m_i > 1mi​>1 and αi∈[0,C]\alpha_i\in[0, C]αi​∈[0,C] if mi=1m_i = 1mi​=1: a step function of the margin, which is a hardened version of the smooth sigmoid Cσ(−mi)C\sigma(-m_i)Cσ(−mi​). We can check the identity on the Breast Cancer data.

logit_b = LogisticRegression(C=C_b, tol=1e-12, max_iter=100_000).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
w_l, b_l = logit_b.coef_.ravel(), logit_b.intercept_[0]
m_l = sb * (Zb @ w_l + b_l)
alpha_l = C_b / (1 + np.exp(m_l))                                         # C * sigmoid(-m_i)
print(f"logistic regression, C = {C_b}: largest |w - sum alpha_i y_i x_i| = {np.abs(w_l - (alpha_l * sb) @ Zb).max():.1e}, sum alpha_i y_i = {alpha_l @ sb:.1e}")
cosine = w_b @ w_l / (np.linalg.norm(w_b) * np.linalg.norm(w_l))
print(f"cosine between the SVM weights and the logistic weights: {cosine:.4f};  norms {np.linalg.norm(w_b):.3f} and {np.linalg.norm(w_l):.3f}")
print(f"examples with a non-zero multiplier: SVM {int((alpha_b > 1e-9).sum())} of {n_b};  "
      f"logistic: {int((alpha_l > 1e-3 * C_b).sum())} with alpha_i > 0.001 C, {int((alpha_l > 1e-6 * C_b).sum())} with alpha_i > 1e-6 C, {int((alpha_l > 0).sum())} with alpha_i > 0")
print(f"test accuracy: SVM {np.mean(np.sign(svm_b.decision_function(Zb_te)) == sb_te):.4f}, logistic {logit_b.score(Zb_te, yb_te):.4f}")
logistic regression, C = 1.0: largest |w - sum alpha_i y_i x_i| = 2.0e-06, sum alpha_i y_i = -9.8e-07
cosine between the SVM weights and the logistic weights: 0.9189;  norms 2.712 and 3.764
examples with a non-zero multiplier: SVM 36 of 426;  logistic: 228 with alpha_i > 0.001 C, 387 with alpha_i > 1e-6 C, 426 with alpha_i > 0
test accuracy: SVM 0.9580, logistic 0.9650

The identity holds to the precision of the solver (2⋅10−62\cdot 10^{-6}2⋅10−6): the regularized logistic regression is also a combination of training examples with ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0, but no multiplier is exactly zero. For the same C=1C = 1C=1 the logistic regression has 228 examples with αi>0.001 C\alpha_i > 0.001\,Cαi​>0.001C and 387 with αi>10−6C\alpha_i > 10^{-6}Cαi​>10−6C, against 36 for the SVM (20 free and 16 bounded). The two weight vectors point in similar directions (cosine 0.919; norms 2.71 for the SVM and 3.76 for the logistic regression) and give the same kind of accuracy on the test set, 0.958 and 0.965 (6 and 5 errors among 143 patients). The difference between the two methods is therefore not in what they can express but in how the training set is used: the SVM needs only its support vectors, which gives a compact model and the leave-one-out bound of Section 8.6, while the logistic regression keeps a small weight on every example and delivers probabilities. When the data are separable and C→∞C\to\inftyC→∞, the direction of the logistic solution converges to the hard-margin direction (Section 7.7.3 reached it from the side of gradient descent), because the margins of the non-support examples grow, so that their weights Cσ(−mi)C\sigma(-m_i)Cσ(−mi​) vanish.

8.4.2 What the hinge loss estimates¶

Chapter 6 chose the logistic loss because it is the negative log-likelihood of a model of the conditional probability, and the classifier it produces estimates η(x)=P(y=1∣x)\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{P}(y = 1\mid\mathbf{x})η(x)=P(y=1∣x) (through σ(f(x))\sigma(f(\mathbf{x}))σ(f(x))). The hinge loss has no such interpretation, and the next result says what it does instead. Let fff be an arbitrary function of x\mathbf{x}x (not necessarily linear), and write η(x)=P(y=+1∣x)\eta(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{P}(y = +1\mid\mathbf{x})η(x)=P(y=+1∣x), as in Chapter 3, so that the Bayes classifier is sign⁡(η(x)−12)\operatorname{sign}(\eta(\mathbf{x}) - \tfrac12)sign(η(x)−21​).

Proposition 8.5 (the population minimizer of the hinge loss is the Bayes classifier)

For every x\mathbf{x}x with η(x)≠12\eta(\mathbf{x})\ne\tfrac12η(x)=21​, the value f(x)f(\mathbf{x})f(x) that minimizes the conditional expected hinge loss η ℓhinge(f)+(1−η) ℓhinge(−f)\eta\,\ell_{\text{hinge}}(f) + (1 - \eta)\,\ell_{\text{hinge}}(-f)ηℓhinge​(f)+(1−η)ℓhinge​(−f) is f∗(x)=sign⁡(2η(x)−1)f^\ast(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{sign}(2\eta(\mathbf{x}) - 1)f∗(x)=sign(2η(x)−1): the hinge loss estimates the Bayes classifier directly and not the probability. For comparison, the minimizer of the logistic loss log⁡(1+e−m)\log(1 + e^{-m})log(1+e−m) is f∗=ln⁡η1−ηf^\ast = \ln\frac{\eta}{1 - \eta}f∗=ln1−ηη​ (the log-odds) and that of the squared hinge loss is f∗=2η−1f^\ast = 2\eta - 1f∗=2η−1 for η∈[0,1]\eta \in [0, 1]η∈[0,1] (Exercise 8.3).

Proof

Fix x\mathbf{x}x and write η\etaη for η(x)\eta(\mathbf{x})η(x) and g(f)=ηmax⁡{0,1−f}+(1−η)max⁡{0,1+f}g(f) = \eta\max\{0, 1 - f\} + (1 - \eta)\max\{0, 1 + f\}g(f)=ηmax{0,1−f}+(1−η)max{0,1+f}. For f∈[−1,1]f\in[-1, 1]f∈[−1,1] both maxima are linear: g(f)=η(1−f)+(1−η)(1+f)=1+(1−2η)fg(f) = \eta(1 - f) + (1 - \eta)(1 + f) = 1 + (1 - 2\eta)fg(f)=η(1−f)+(1−η)(1+f)=1+(1−2η)f, which is decreasing in fff when η>12\eta > \tfrac12η>21​ (and increasing when η<12\eta < \tfrac12η<21​). For f>1f > 1f>1 we have g(f)=(1−η)(1+f)g(f) = (1 - \eta)(1 + f)g(f)=(1−η)(1+f), increasing in fff, and for f<−1f < -1f<−1 we have g(f)=η(1−f)g(f) = \eta(1 - f)g(f)=η(1−f), decreasing in fff. Thus if η>12\eta > \tfrac12η>21​ the function ggg decreases on (−∞,1](-\infty, 1](−∞,1] and increases on [1,∞)[1, \infty)[1,∞), and its unique minimizer is f=1f = 1f=1, with value 2(1−η)2(1 - \eta)2(1−η). The case η<12\eta < \tfrac12η<21​ is symmetric and gives f=−1f = -1f=−1. □\square□

Two consequences. First, the Bayes classifier is the best classifier of Chapter 3 (the minimizer of the 0–1 risk), and the hinge loss reaches it in the limit of a rich enough class and of unlimited data: a surrogate with this property is called classification-calibrated, and Zhang (2004) shows that the excess 0–1 risk is bounded by the excess hinge risk, R(f)−R∗≤Rhinge(f)−Rhinge∗\mathcal{R}(f) - \mathcal{R}^\ast\le\mathcal{R}_{\text{hinge}}(f) - \mathcal{R}^\ast_{\text{hinge}}R(f)−R∗≤Rhinge​(f)−Rhinge∗​. Second, the score of an SVM is not a probability: it is a distance to the hyperplane, whose size depends on CCC, and since f∗f^\astf∗ takes the value ±1\pm 1±1 whatever the confidence, the scores carry no calibrated information about η\etaη. If probabilities are needed they must be added in a second step (Platt scaling, Section 8.7.3), by the recalibration of Section 5.6.4.

8.5 Solving the SVM¶

The SVM is a convex quadratic program, and a general-purpose solver could handle it, as in the cells above for the primal. The structure of the problem allows much better algorithms, which we derive and implement from scratch in this section. They belong to the two families of Chapter 7: a first-order method on the primal (the hinge loss is not differentiable, so it needs subgradients), and a coordinate method on the dual (where the constraints are simple boxes).

8.5.1 The subgradient method¶

The hinge loss has a kink at m=1m = 1m=1, and the theorems of Chapter 7, which assume an LLL-smooth function, do not apply. A subgradient of a convex function fff at w\mathbf{w}w is any vector g\mathbf{g}g with f(v)≥f(w)+g⊤(v−w)f(\mathbf{v})\ge f(\mathbf{w}) + \mathbf{g}^\top(\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{w})f(v)≥f(w)+g⊤(v−w) for all v\mathbf{v}v; at a point where fff is differentiable it is the gradient, and at a kink it is any slope between the left and right derivatives. For the objective f(w)=1n∑imax⁡{0,1−yiw⊤xi}+λ2∥w∥2f(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1n\sum_i\max\{0, 1 - y_i\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i\} + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2f(w)=n1​∑i​max{0,1−yi​w⊤xi​}+2λ​∥w∥2 a subgradient is

g(w)=λw−1n∑i : yiw⊤xi<1yixi,\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{w}) = \lambda\mathbf{w} - \frac1n\sum_{i\,:\,y_i\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i < 1}y_i\mathbf{x}_i,g(w)=λw−n1​i:yi​w⊤xi​<1∑​yi​xi​,
(13)

which differs from a gradient only through the convention at the kinks (we take 0 for the examples with margin exactly 1). It is the same “features times residual” structure as in Chapter 7, with a residual that is 1 for the examples inside the margin and 0 for the others. To have a strongly convex objective we put the intercept inside w\mathbf{w}w (as a constant feature) and therefore penalize it; this is the form that LinearSVC solves, and Section 8.5.3 comments on the difference.

Theorem 8.6 (the subgradient method with step 1/(λk)1/(\lambda k)1/(λk))

Let fff be λ\lambdaλ-strongly convex on a closed convex set Ω\OmegaΩ, with minimizer w∗∈Ω\mathbf{w}^\ast\in\Omegaw∗∈Ω, and let wk+1=ΠΩ(wk−ηkgk)\mathbf{w}_{k+1} = \Pi_\Omega\big(\mathbf{w}_k - \eta_k\mathbf{g}_k\big)wk+1​=ΠΩ​(wk​−ηk​gk​) with gk∈∂f(wk)\mathbf{g}_k\in\partial f(\mathbf{w}_k)gk​∈∂f(wk​) (where ΠΩ\Pi_\OmegaΠΩ​ is the projection on Ω\OmegaΩ), the step ηk=1/(λk)\eta_k = 1/(\lambda k)ηk​=1/(λk), and ∥gk∥≤G\lVert\mathbf{g}_k\rVert\le G∥gk​∥≤G for all kkk. Then for every K≥1K\ge 1K≥1

Compare with Chapter 7. For a smooth and strongly convex function gradient descent converges at the linear rate (1−μ/L)k(1 - \mu/L)^k(1−μ/L)k (Theorem 7.5); for the non-smooth hinge loss the best that this method guarantees is O(ln⁡K/K)O(\ln K/K)O(lnK/K): the price of the kink. The stochastic version, which replaces gk\mathbf{g}_kgk​ by the subgradient of a single example, gk=λwk−yixiI[yiwk⊤xi<1]\mathbf{g}_k = \lambda\mathbf{w}_k - y_i\mathbf{x}_i\mathbb{I}[y_i\mathbf{w}_k^\top\mathbf{x}_i < 1]gk​=λwk​−yi​xi​I[yi​wk⊤​xi​<1], is the Pegasos algorithm of Shalev-Shwartz et al. (2011); the proof above holds in expectation, because the expected stochastic subgradient is a subgradient and G2G^2G2 bounds E∥gk∥2\mathbb{E}\lVert\mathbf{g}_k\rVert^2E∥gk​∥2. The cost of an iteration does not depend on nnn, which is the point of Section 7.6. The bound has the typical form G2λ⋅ln⁡KK\tfrac{G^2}{\lambda}\cdot\tfrac{\ln K}{K}λG2​⋅KlnK​, in which the strong convexity λ=1/(Cn)\lambda = 1/(Cn)λ=1/(Cn) appears in the denominator: the larger CCC and nnn, the weaker the regularization and the slower the convergence.

To measure the rate we need the exact minimum f∗f^\astf∗ of the problem with the intercept inside w\mathbf{w}w. We compute it with the dual coordinate descent of Hsieh et al. (2008), which is also the algorithm of LinearSVC: with the intercept in w\mathbf{w}w the equality constraint of the dual disappears, only the boxes 0≤αi≤C0\le\alpha_i\le C0≤αi​≤C remain, and the function of a single αi\alpha_iαi​ (the others fixed) is a one-dimensional quadratic, whose minimizer is the Newton step clipped to the box. The cell below implements it, checks the duality gap, and then runs the subgradient method, deterministic (all the examples at each step) for 104 steps and stochastic (one example) for 2⋅1052\cdot 10^52⋅105 steps. The domain is the ball of radius 2/λ\sqrt{2/\lambda}2/λ​, which contains the minimizer because λ2∥w∗∥2≤f(w∗)≤f(0)=1\frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2\le f(\mathbf{w}^\ast)\le f(\mathbf{0}) = 12λ​∥w∗∥2≤f(w∗)≤f(0)=1.

def dual_coordinate_descent(A, s, C, tol=1e-9, max_sweeps=5000, seed=SEED):
    """Dual coordinate descent for  min 1/2||w||^2 + C sum_i max(0, 1 - s_i w.a_i)  (intercept inside w): boxes only."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(s)
    alpha, w = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(A.shape[1])
    q = np.einsum("ij,ij->i", A, A)                                       # Q_ii = ||a_i||^2
    for sweep in range(1, max_sweeps + 1):
        for i in rng.permutation(n):
            g = s[i] * (w @ A[i]) - 1                                     # derivative of the (minimized) dual in alpha_i
            new = min(max(alpha[i] - g / q[i], 0.0), C)                   # Newton step, clipped to the box [0, C]
            w += (new - alpha[i]) * s[i] * A[i]
            alpha[i] = new
        if sweep % 10 == 0:
            primal = 0.5 * w @ w + C * np.maximum(0, 1 - s * (A @ w)).sum()
            dual = alpha.sum() - 0.5 * w @ w
            if (primal - dual) / (n * C) < tol:
                break
    return w, alpha, sweep, (primal - dual) / (n * C)


lam_b = 1 / (n_b * C_b)
A_b = np.c_[np.ones(n_b), Zb]                                             # the constant feature: the intercept is inside w (and penalized)


def f_hinge(w):
    return 0.5 * lam_b * w @ w + np.mean(np.maximum(0, 1 - sb * (A_b @ w)))


w_dcd, alpha_dcd, sweeps_dcd, gap_dcd = dual_coordinate_descent(A_b, sb, C_b)
f_star_b = f_hinge(w_dcd)
print(f"dual coordinate descent: {sweeps_dcd} sweeps, duality gap {gap_dcd:.1e}, f* = {f_star_b:.8f}, ||w*|| = {np.linalg.norm(w_dcd):.4f}, "
      f"support vectors {int((alpha_dcd > 0).sum())} ({int((alpha_dcd >= C_b - 1e-9).sum())} at the bound), lambda = {lam_b:.2e}")


def subgradient_method(T, stochastic, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    radius = np.sqrt(2 / lam_b)                                           # the minimizer lies in this ball since f(0) = 1
    w, w_avg = np.zeros(A_b.shape[1]), np.zeros(A_b.shape[1])
    checkpoints = set(np.unique(np.round(np.logspace(0, np.log10(T), 45)).astype(int))) | {10, 100, 1000, 10_000, 100_000, 200_000}
    record, g_max = [], 0.0
    for t in range(1, T + 1):
        if stochastic:
            i = rng.integers(n_b)
            g = lam_b * w - (sb[i] * A_b[i] if sb[i] * (A_b[i] @ w) < 1 else 0.0)
        else:
            viol = sb * (A_b @ w) < 1
            g = lam_b * w - (sb[viol, None] * A_b[viol]).sum(axis=0) / n_b
        g_max = max(g_max, np.linalg.norm(g))
        w = w - g / (lam_b * t)                                           # the step 1 / (lambda t) of Theorem 8.6
        norm = np.linalg.norm(w)
        if norm > radius:
            w *= radius / norm                                            # projection on the ball
        w_avg += (w - w_avg) / t                                          # running average of the iterates
        if t in checkpoints:
            record.append((t, f_hinge(w) - f_star_b, f_hinge(w_avg) - f_star_b))
    return np.array(record), g_max


rec_full, g_full = subgradient_method(10_000, stochastic=False)
rec_sgd, g_sgd = subgradient_method(200_000, stochastic=True)

Against this exact value the tables and Figure 8.5(a) show the subgradient method. The deterministic method is 2.3⋅10−32.3\cdot 10^{-3}2.3⋅10−3 above the minimum after 100 steps, 2.0⋅10−42.0\cdot 10^{-4}2.0⋅10−4 after 1,0001{,}0001,000 and 3.9⋅10−53.9\cdot 10^{-5}3.9⋅10−5 after 104 for the last iterate; the average of the iterates, which is the object of Theorem 8.6, is 6.1⋅10−26.1\cdot 10^{-2}6.1⋅10−2, 3.8⋅10−33.8\cdot 10^{-3}3.8⋅10−3 and 3.7⋅10−43.7\cdot 10^{-4}3.7⋅10−4 at the same steps, an order of magnitude worse because it carries the large early errors, but it decays like 1/k1/k1/k (up to the logarithm), as the theorem says. The bound itself, computed with the largest subgradient norm met along the run (2.78), is true and loose by three to four orders of magnitude (1.7 at k=104k = 10^4k=104, against 3.7⋅10−43.7\cdot 10^{-4}3.7⋅10−4 for the average iterate and 3.9⋅10−53.9\cdot 10^{-5}3.9⋅10−5 for the last one), the typical fate of worst-case bounds, as for Theorem 7.4. The stochastic method makes one cheap step per example: its suboptimality is 1.7⋅10−11.7\cdot 10^{-1}1.7⋅10−1 after 1,0001{,}0001,000 steps, 2.3⋅10−22.3\cdot 10^{-2}2.3⋅10−2 after 104 (23 epochs), 1.9⋅10−31.9\cdot 10^{-3}1.9⋅10−3 after 105 (234 epochs) and 9⋅10−49\cdot 10^{-4}9⋅10−4 after 2⋅1052\cdot 10^52⋅105 steps (470 epochs); the same decay in the number of steps but with the irregular jumps of SGD. Counted in passes over the data, the deterministic method is better on this small problem (2.3⋅10−32.3\cdot 10^{-3}2.3⋅10−3 after 100 epochs, against 1.9⋅10−31.9\cdot 10^{-3}1.9⋅10−3 after 234), the conclusion of Section 7.6 for Breast Cancer: stochastic methods win when nnn is large, not when it is 426.

8.5.2 Sequential minimal optimization¶

The subgradient method treats the primal; it converges slowly because of the kink. The dual is a smooth quadratic program in α\boldsymbol\alphaα with box constraints and the equality constraint ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0 (when the intercept is kept out of the norm). A coordinate method that moves a single αi\alpha_iαi​ would violate the equality, so the smallest feasible move changes two multipliers at once. This is the idea of sequential minimal optimization (SMO, Platt, 1998), which underlies libsvm, and the two-variable subproblem can be solved in closed form.

Write the dual as the minimization of D(α)=12α⊤Qα−1⊤αD(\boldsymbol\alpha) = \frac12\boldsymbol\alpha^\top\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol\alpha - \mathbf{1}^\top\boldsymbol\alphaD(α)=21​α⊤Qα−1⊤α with Qij=yiyjKijQ_{ij} = y_iy_jK_{ij}Qij​=yi​yj​Kij​ and Kij=xi⊤xjK_{ij} = \mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jKij​=xi⊤​xj​ (the Gram matrix; with other functions of xi,xj\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_jxi​,xj​ in its place we obtain the kernels of Chapter 9). Let f0(xt)=∑sαsysKstf_0(\mathbf{x}_t) = \sum_s\alpha_sy_sK_{st}f0​(xt​)=∑s​αs​ys​Kst​ be the score without intercept and et=yt−f0(xt)e_t = y_t - f_0(\mathbf{x}_t)et​=yt​−f0​(xt​). The gradient of DDD is ∇tD=ytf0(xt)−1=−ytet\nabla_tD = y_tf_0(\mathbf{x}_t) - 1 = -y_te_t∇t​D=yt​f0​(xt​)−1=−yt​et​.

Proposition 8.7 (optimality and the SMO step)

Let Iup={t:(yt=1,αt<C) or (yt=−1,αt>0)}I_{\text{up}} = \{t : (y_t = 1, \alpha_t < C)\ \text{or}\ (y_t = -1, \alpha_t > 0)\}Iup​={t:(yt​=1,αt​<C) or (yt​=−1,αt​>0)} and Ilow={t:(yt=1,αt>0) or (yt=−1,αt<C)}I_{\text{low}} = \{t : (y_t = 1, \alpha_t > 0)\ \text{or}\ (y_t = -1, \alpha_t < C)\}Ilow​={t:(yt​=1,αt​>0) or (yt​=−1,αt​<C)}. If i∈Iupi\in I_{\text{up}}i∈Iup​ and j∈Ilowj\in I_{\text{low}}j∈Ilow​ violate it (gap=ei−ej>0\text{gap} = e_i - e_j > 0gap=ei​−ej​>0), the move αi↦αi+yit\alpha_i\mapsto\alpha_i + y_itαi​↦αi​+yi​t, αj↦αj−yjt\alpha_j\mapsto\alpha_j - y_jtαj​↦αj​−yj​t keeps ∑sαsys\sum_s\alpha_sy_s∑s​αs​ys​ constant, and DDD is minimized along it, for t≥0t\ge 0t≥0, at

t∗=min⁡{ ei−ejKii+Kjj−2Kij,  tmax⁡},t^\ast = \min\Big\{\ \frac{e_i - e_j}{K_{ii} + K_{jj} - 2K_{ij}},\ \ t_{\max}\Big\},t∗=min{ Kii​+Kjj​−2Kij​ei​−ej​​,  tmax​},
(17)

where tmax⁡t_{\max}tmax​ is the largest ttt for which αi\alpha_iαi​ and αj\alpha_jαj​ remain in [0,C][0, C][0,C]. The dual objective decreases at every step in which gap>0\text{gap} > 0gap>0.

Proof

Optimality. The KKT conditions of Theorem 8.4 say that for some bbb: yt(f0(xt)+b)≥1y_t(f_0(\mathbf{x}_t) + b)\ge 1yt​(f0​(xt​)+b)≥1 if αt=0\alpha_t = 0αt​=0, =1= 1=1 if 0<αt<C0 < \alpha_t < C0<αt​<C, and ≤1\le 1≤1 if αt=C\alpha_t = Cαt​=C. Written with et=yt−f0(xt)e_t = y_t - f_0(\mathbf{x}_t)et​=yt​−f0​(xt​) (multiply by yty_tyt​, using yt2=1y_t^2 = 1yt2​=1) these are: et≤be_t\le bet​≤b for yt=1y_t = 1yt​=1 and αt<C\alpha_t < Cαt​<C, and for yt=−1y_t = -1yt​=−1 and αt>0\alpha_t > 0αt​>0 (that is, for t∈Iupt\in I_{\text{up}}t∈Iup​); et≥be_t\ge bet​≥b for t∈Ilowt\in I_{\text{low}}t∈Ilow​; and et=be_t = bet​=b for the free examples (which are in both sets). Such a bbb exists if and only if max⁡Iupet≤min⁡Ilowet\max_{I_{\text{up}}}e_t\le\min_{I_{\text{low}}}e_tmaxIup​​et​≤minIlow​​et​. The step. Along the direction d\mathbf{d}d with di=yid_i = y_idi​=yi​, dj=−yjd_j = -y_jdj​=−yj​ and all other entries zero, y⊤d=yi2−yj2=0\mathbf{y}^\top\mathbf{d} = y_i^2 - y_j^2 = 0y⊤d=yi2​−yj2​=0, so the equality constraint is preserved. The directional derivative of DDD is ∇iD yi−∇jD yj=−ei+ej=−gap<0\nabla_iD\,y_i - \nabla_jD\,y_j = -e_i + e_j = -\text{gap} < 0∇i​Dyi​−∇j​Dyj​=−ei​+ej​=−gap<0, and the curvature is d⊤Qd=Qii+Qjj−2yiyjQij=Kii+Kjj−2Kij=∥ϕ(xi)−ϕ(xj)∥2\mathbf{d}^\top\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{d} = Q_{ii} + Q_{jj} - 2y_iy_jQ_{ij} = K_{ii} + K_{jj} - 2K_{ij} = \lVert\phi(\mathbf{x}_i) - \phi(\mathbf{x}_j)\rVert^2d⊤Qd=Qii​+Qjj​−2yi​yj​Qij​=Kii​+Kjj​−2Kij​=∥ϕ(xi​)−ϕ(xj​)∥2, which is positive for distinct points. The minimum of the quadratic t↦D(α+td)t\mapsto D(\boldsymbol\alpha + t\mathbf{d})t↦D(α+td) is at gap/(Kii+Kjj−2Kij)\text{gap}/(K_{ii} + K_{jj} - 2K_{ij})gap/(Kii​+Kjj​−2Kij​) and, the function being convex, the minimizer on an interval of feasible values is this point clipped to the interval. The directions of the sets IupI_{\text{up}}Iup​ and IlowI_{\text{low}}Ilow​ are exactly those that increase αi\alpha_iαi​ (or decrease it, according to yiy_iyi​) without leaving the box, so tmax⁡>0t_{\max} > 0tmax​>0. □\square□

Choosing the pair with the largest violation (the maximal eie_iei​ in IupI_{\text{up}}Iup​ and the minimal eje_jej​ in IlowI_{\text{low}}Ilow​) gives the simplest version of the algorithm, and the stopping rule is gap≤ε\text{gap}\le\varepsilongap≤ε. The cell below is the whole algorithm. It works with the Gram matrix, so it will handle kernels without changes.

def smo(K, y, C, tol=1e-8, max_iter=500_000, record=False):
    """Sequential minimal optimization (maximal violating pair) for the SVM dual with a Gram matrix K and labels in {-1, +1}."""
    n = len(y)
    alpha, G = np.zeros(n), -np.ones(n)                                   # G = Q alpha - 1 is the gradient of the dual
    hist = []
    for it in range(1, max_iter + 1):
        e = -y * G                                                        # e_t = y_t - f_0(x_t)
        up = ((y == 1) & (alpha < C)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha > 0))
        low = ((y == 1) & (alpha > 0)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha < C))
        i = np.flatnonzero(up)[np.argmax(e[up])]
        j = np.flatnonzero(low)[np.argmin(e[low])]
        gap = e[i] - e[j]
        if record:
            hist.append((gap, 0.5 * alpha.sum() - 0.5 * alpha @ G))       # violation and dual value  sum(alpha) - 1/2 alpha Q alpha
        if gap <= tol:
            break
        a = max(K[i, i] + K[j, j] - 2 * K[i, j], 1e-12)
        t_i = (C - alpha[i]) if y[i] == 1 else alpha[i]                   # room to move alpha_i along y_i
        t_j = alpha[j] if y[j] == 1 else (C - alpha[j])                   # room to move alpha_j along -y_j
        t = min(gap / a, t_i, t_j)
        d_i, d_j = y[i] * t, -y[j] * t
        alpha[i] += d_i
        alpha[j] += d_j
        G += (y * y[i]) * K[:, i] * d_i + (y * y[j]) * K[:, j] * d_j      # update of the gradient: two columns of Q
    e = -y * G
    free = (alpha > 1e-10) & (alpha < C - 1e-10)
    if free.any():
        b = e[free].mean()                                                # e_t = b for the free support vectors
    else:
        up = ((y == 1) & (alpha < C)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha > 0))
        low = ((y == 1) & (alpha > 0)) | ((y == -1) & (alpha < C))
        b = (e[up].max() + e[low].min()) / 2
    return alpha, b, it, (np.array(hist) if record else None)


K_b = Zb @ Zb.T                                                           # linear Gram matrix of the 426 training patients
rows = []
for C in [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 1000]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    a_, b_, iters_, _ = smo(K_b, sb, C, tol=1e-9)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    ref = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-10).fit(Zb, sb)
    w_ = (a_ * sb) @ Zb
    rows.append({"C": C, "SMO iterations": iters_, "support vectors (SMO)": int((a_ > 1e-9).sum()), "support vectors (SVC)": len(ref.support_),
                 "rel. diff. of w": np.linalg.norm(w_ - ref.coef_.ravel()) / np.linalg.norm(ref.coef_), "|b - b_SVC|": abs(b_ - ref.intercept_[0])})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2e}" if v < 1e-2 else f"{v:.4g}"))

0.01             326                    101                    101         1.02e-08     1.12e-08
 0.1            3281                     51                     51         1.79e-07     1.18e-07

For C=1C = 1C=1 the algorithm stops, with a violation below 10-9, after 20,89920{,}89920,899 iterations, with the same 36 support vectors as libsvm, and the weights and the intercept agree with those of SVC to 10-6 (relative): the agreement is limited by the tolerance of the reference solver, not by ours. The number of iterations grows with CCC (326 for C=0.01C = 0.01C=0.01, 198,021198{,}021198,021 for C=1000C = 1000C=1000): the problems with weak regularization are the hard ones, as in Theorem 8.6, where λ=1/(Cn)\lambda = 1/(Cn)λ=1/(Cn) divides the bound. libsvm needs 9,5249{,}5249,524 iterations for C=1C = 1C=1 (see the table below): it chooses the second index of the pair with a second-order criterion, which uses the curvature Kii+Kjj−2KijK_{ii} + K_{jj} - 2K_{ij}Kii​+Kjj​−2Kij​ of the quadratic instead of only the violation. Figure 8.5(b) shows the two phases typical of the method. In the first, about 103 iterations, the algorithm identifies which multipliers are at 0, at CCC or free, and the dual value hardly moves; in the second the dual suboptimality drops by about ten orders of magnitude over the next 2⋅1042\cdot 10^42⋅104 iterations, while the violation, which is not monotone, follows with a delay. An SMO iteration updates two columns of the Gram matrix, O(n)O(n)O(n) operations, while a subgradient step on the primal costs O(np)O(np)O(np): the dual is the right object to work on when ppp is large or when the Gram matrix comes from a kernel and ppp is not even defined.

# Figure 8.5 — the two solvers: subgradient method (primal) and SMO (dual)
_, _, it_smo, hist_smo = smo(K_b, sb, C_b, tol=1e-9, record=True)
dual_star = hist_smo[-1, 1]

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.6, 4.2))

    ax.loglog(rec_full[:, 0], rec_full[:, 2], color=BLUE, lw=1.8, ls="--", label="deterministic, average")
