8.5.3 What the libraries do¶

scikit-learn offers three implementations of the linear SVM, which solve slightly different problems.

EstimatorAlgorithmInterceptKernelsCost
SVC(kernel="linear")libsvm: SMO with a second-order choice of the pairfree (outside the norm), as in this chapteryes (Chapter 9)between O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) and O(n3)O(n^3)O(n3) time, O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) cache of the Gram matrix
LinearSVCliblinear: dual coordinate descent (or a primal Newton method)penalized (a constant feature, scaled by intercept_scaling)noO(np)O(np)O(np) per sweep, fast for large nnn
SGDClassifier(loss="hinge")stochastic subgradient (Section 7.6) with a decreasing stepfreenoO(p)O(p)O(p) per update, a few epochs

The intercept is the source of small differences between the results. The cell below fits the same problem (C=1C = 1C=1, Breast Cancer) with the four variants and compares the weights with those of SVC.

ref_w, ref_b = svm_b.coef_.ravel(), svm_b.intercept_[0]
variants = {
    "SVC (libsvm), intercept free": svm_b,
    "LinearSVC, hinge, intercept_scaling = 1": LinearSVC(C=C_b, loss="hinge", dual=True, max_iter=1_000_000, tol=1e-8).fit(Zb, sb),
    "LinearSVC, hinge, intercept_scaling = 10": LinearSVC(C=C_b, loss="hinge", dual=True, intercept_scaling=10, max_iter=1_000_000, tol=1e-8).fit(Zb, sb),
    "SGDClassifier, hinge, 2000 epochs": SGDClassifier(loss="hinge", alpha=1 / (C_b * n_b), max_iter=2000, tol=None, random_state=SEED).fit(Zb, sb),
    "LinearSVC, squared hinge": LinearSVC(C=C_b, loss="squared_hinge", dual=True, max_iter=1_000_000, tol=1e-8).fit(Zb, sb),
}
rows = []
for name, m_ in variants.items():
    w_, b_ = m_.coef_.ravel(), m_.intercept_[0]
    rows.append({"variant": name, "||w||": np.linalg.norm(w_), "b": b_, "rel. distance of w from SVC": np.linalg.norm(w_ - ref_w) / np.linalg.norm(ref_w),
                 "test accuracy": np.mean(np.sign(Zb_te @ w_ + b_) == sb_te), "iterations": float(np.ravel(getattr(m_, "n_iter_", np.nan))[0])})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}" if abs(v) < 1e4 else f"{v:.0f}"))
                                 variant  ||w||       b  rel. distance of w from SVC  test accuracy  iterations
            SVC (libsvm), intercept free 2.7119 -0.0505                       0.0000         0.9580   9620.0000
 LinearSVC, hinge, intercept_scaling = 1 2.7177 -0.0422                       0.0065         0.9580   5764.0000
LinearSVC, hinge, intercept_scaling = 10 2.7119 -0.0504                       0.0001         0.9580       78421
       SGDClassifier, hinge, 2000 epochs 2.7264 -0.0454                       0.0121         0.9580   2000.0000
                LinearSVC, squared hinge 3.0407  0.2192                       0.5017         0.9650    869.0000

The four hinge-loss solutions agree to within 1.2%1.2\%1.2% in their weights and have the same test accuracy (0.958), and the differences come from details of the problem, not from the algorithm. LinearSVC penalizes the intercept, and its solution is 0.65%0.65\%0.65% away from that of SVC; with intercept_scaling=10 the intercept is penalized 100 times less and the distance falls to 0.01%0.01\%0.01%, but liblinear then needs 72,49372{,}49372,493 iterations instead of 5,4535{,}4535,453: the same trade-off as in Section 7.4, where the scale of one coordinate controls the conditioning of the whole problem. SGDClassifier with 2000 epochs is stochastic and is 1.2%1.2\%1.2% away. The last row is a different model: the squared hinge loss penalizes the violations quadratically, gives a larger norm (3.04) and a different weight vector (50%50\%50% away) and, on this test set, a slightly different accuracy (0.965, one more patient classified correctly): neither is better, since the test set cannot decide. In practice: use SVC when nnn is up to a few tens of thousands (it is the only one that handles kernels), and LinearSVC or SGDClassifier for large nnn with a linear model.

8.6 Why the margin matters: generalization¶

8.6.1 The margin bound, evaluated¶

Theorem 3.7 said that, with probability at least 1−δ1 - \delta1−δ, all linear classifiers w⊤x\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}w⊤x with ∥w∥≤B\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert\le B∥w∥≤B on data with ∥x∥≤R\lVert\mathbf{x}\rVert\le R∥x∥≤R satisfy

P(y w⊤x≤0) ≤ 1n#{i:yiw⊤xi<γ}+2BRγn+ln⁡(1/δ)2n.\mathbb{P}\big(y\,\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}\le 0\big)\ \le\ \frac1n\#\{i : y_i\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i < \gamma\} + \frac{2BR}{\gamma\sqrt n} + \sqrt{\frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{2n}} .P(yw⊤x≤0) ≤ n1​#{i:yi​w⊤xi​<γ}+γn​2BR​+2nln(1/δ)​​.
(18)

The SVM is built to make this expression small: the constraints yif(xi)≥1y_i f(\mathbf{x}_i)\ge 1yi​f(xi​)≥1 make the first term small (γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1), and minimizing ∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥ makes BBB small; the parameter CCC trades the two. To apply the theorem with an intercept we use the augmented vectors x~=(1,x)\tilde{\mathbf{x}} = (1, \mathbf{x})x~=(1,x) and w~=(b,w)\tilde{\mathbf{w}} = (b, \mathbf{w})w~=(b,w), so that B=∥w~∥B = \lVert\tilde{\mathbf{w}}\rVertB=∥w~∥ and R=max⁡i∥x~i∥R = \max_i\lVert\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i\rVertR=maxi​∥x~i​∥. Strictly, BBB must be fixed before seeing the data; using the value found by the algorithm costs a union bound over a grid of values of BBB, which adds a small term that we ignore. The cell evaluates the bound on the Breast Cancer training set for several values of CCC. As in Section 3.8.3, we also compute the variant in which the worst-case radius RRR is replaced by the root-mean-square norm of the sample, RrmsR_{\text{rms}}Rrms​: this is not what Theorem 3.7 states (the outlier radius is what the proof needs), but it is the data-dependent form that Section 3.8.3 found to be much tighter, and it is useful as a heuristic.

Zb_aug = np.c_[np.ones(n_b), Zb]                                           # augmented vectors (1, x)
R_max = np.linalg.norm(Zb_aug, axis=1).max()
R_rms = np.sqrt(np.mean(np.sum(Zb_aug**2, axis=1)))
conf_term = np.sqrt(np.log(1 / 0.05) / (2 * n_b))                          # delta = 0.05
print(f"R (largest norm) = {R_max:.2f}, R_rms = {R_rms:.2f}, confidence term = {conf_term:.3f}")
rows = []
for C in [0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 1, 1000]:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-9).fit(Zb, sb)
    w_, b_ = m_.coef_.ravel(), m_.intercept_[0]
    B = np.sqrt(w_ @ w_ + b_**2)
    frac = np.mean(sb * (Zb @ w_ + b_) < 1 - 1e-6)                         # fraction of training points with margin below gamma = 1
    cap_max, cap_rms = 2 * B * R_max / np.sqrt(n_b), 2 * B * R_rms / np.sqrt(n_b)
    rows.append({"C": C, "B": B, "below margin": frac, "capacity (R)": cap_max, "capacity (R_rms)": cap_rms,
                 "bound (R)": frac + cap_max + conf_term, "bound (R_rms)": frac + cap_rms + conf_term,
                 "test error": np.mean(np.sign(Zb_te @ w_ + b_) != sb_te)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))
R (largest norm) = 19.58, R_rms = 5.57, confidence term = 0.059
       C      B  below margin  capacity (R)  capacity (R_rms)  bound (R)  bound (R_rms)  test error
   0.010  0.767         0.218         1.455             0.414      1.733          0.691       0.042
   0.030  1.034         0.146         1.961             0.558      2.166          0.762       0.021
   0.100  1.419         0.092         2.692             0.766      2.843          0.916       0.021
   1.000  2.712         0.040         5.146             1.463      5.245          1.563       0.042
1000.000 28.408         0.035        53.898            15.327     53.992         15.421       0.070

With the radius RRR of the theorem the bound is above 1.7 for every value of CCC and says nothing: the true error is between 2%2\%2% and 7%7\%7%. The radius is dominated by an outlier patient (R=19.6R = 19.6R=19.6, while the root-mean-square norm is 5.6), and the capacity term 2BR/n2BR/\sqrt n2BR/n​ is between 1.5 and 54 when it should be well below 1 to mean anything. With the heuristic RrmsR_{\text{rms}}Rrms​ the bound falls below 1 for C≤0.1C\le 0.1C≤0.1 (0.69, 0.76, 0.92), is vacuous again at C=1C = 1C=1 (1.56) and absurd for the hard margin (15.4). The numbers are not predictions, but the shape of the bound in CCC is informative. The first term, the fraction of training patients below the margin, falls as CCC grows, from 22%22\%22% to 3.5%3.5\%3.5%; the capacity term grows in proportion to B=∥(w,b)∥B = \lVert(\mathbf{w}, b)\rVertB=∥(w,b)∥, from 0.77 to 28.4 (a factor 37); and the sum is smallest, among the values tried, at the smallest CCC (0.01). The test error is lowest (2.1%2.1\%2.1%) at C=0.03C = 0.03C=0.03 and 0.1, a factor of three to ten above the value that minimizes the bound, and highest for the hard margin (7.0%7.0\%7.0%, ten errors among 143 patients): the hard-margin classifier has no training point below the margin, but its capacity term is the largest of the table. A large margin is not enough; what the theorem controls is the norm of w\mathbf{w}w relative to the radius of the data, and the soft margin gives up some training points to pay for a smaller norm.

8.6.2 A different kind of guarantee: leave-one-out and the support vectors¶

The margin bound is a statement about all classifiers of a class. The sparsity of the SVM gives a very different guarantee, specific to the classifier that the algorithm returns.

Proposition 8.8 (leave-one-out error and support vectors)

Let α^\hat\alphaα^, b^\hat bb^ be a solution of the soft-margin SVM on nnn training examples, with NSV=#{i:α^i>0}N_{\text{SV}} = \#\{i : \hat\alpha_i > 0\}NSV​=#{i:α^i​>0} support vectors. Then the leave-one-out error satisfies

err^LOO=1n∑i=1nI[ yi≠f^(−i)(xi)] ≤ NSVn,\widehat{\mathrm{err}}_{\mathrm{LOO}} = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{I}\big[\,y_i\ne\hat f^{(-i)}(\mathbf{x}_i)\big]\ \le\ \frac{N_{\text{SV}}}{n},errLOO​=n1​i=1∑n​I[yi​=f^​(−i)(xi​)] ≤ nNSV​​,
(19)

where f^(−i)\hat f^{(-i)}f^​(−i) is the SVM trained on the other n−1n - 1n−1 examples (the solution being unique, or any consistent choice among the solutions when it is not).

Proof

Take an example kkk with α^k=0\hat\alpha_k = 0α^k​=0. Remove it, and keep the other multipliers and the same b^\hat bb^. The vector w^=∑i≠kα^iyixi\hat{\mathbf{w}} = \sum_{i\ne k}\hat\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw^=∑i=k​α^i​yi​xi​ is unchanged because the removed term was zero, the constraints 0≤αi≤C0\le\alpha_i\le C0≤αi​≤C and ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0 still hold, and the KKT conditions of Theorem 8.4 for the examples i≠ki\ne ki=k involve only the scores w^⊤xi+b^\hat{\mathbf{w}}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + \hat bw^⊤xi​+b^, which have not changed. Since these conditions are sufficient for optimality, (α^−k,b^)(\hat\alpha_{-k}, \hat b)(α^−k​,b^) is a solution of the SVM trained without example kkk, so f^(−k)=f^\hat f^{(-k)} = \hat ff^​(−k)=f^​ on the examples. Now α^k=0\hat\alpha_k = 0α^k​=0 implies ykf^(xk)≥1>0y_k\hat f(\mathbf{x}_k)\ge 1 > 0yk​f^​(xk​)≥1>0 (Theorem 8.4): the example is classified correctly by f^\hat ff^​, hence by f^(−k)\hat f^{(-k)}f^​(−k). Therefore only support vectors can be leave-one-out errors, and there are NSVN_{\text{SV}}NSV​ of them at most. □\square□

This is a bound that can be computed from the training run, without refitting: like Proposition 6.8 (the leave-one-out shortcut for ridge) it avoids the nnn refits, but it does so through the sparsity of the solution instead of an algebraic identity, and it bounds the error instead of computing it. It is also a statement about the number of support vectors as a measure of the complexity of the solution: the smaller the fraction of support vectors, the better the guarantee, which is a different thing from the number of parameters of the model (which is d+1=31d + 1 = 31d+1=31 here, whatever CCC). We check it on Breast Cancer, for a grid of values of CCC, with the explicit leave-one-out refits (426 per value of CCC) and the 10-fold cross-validation of Chapter 5, and we record the training and test errors. To keep the code short the features are standardized once on the training set, which leaks a negligible amount of information into the validation folds for this comparison; Section 2.7 explains the proper way, a pipeline, which Chapter 5 applies and Section 8.7 uses.

C_grid = np.array([0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10, 30, 100])
skf10 = StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
rows = []
for C in C_grid:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-6).fit(Zb, sb)
    loo_pred = cross_val_predict(SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-6), Zb, sb, cv=LeaveOneOut())
    cv_pred = cross_val_predict(SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-6), Zb, sb, cv=skf10)
    rows.append({"C": C, "support vectors": len(m_.support_), "SV fraction (LOO bound)": len(m_.support_) / n_b,
                 "LOO error": np.mean(loo_pred != sb), "10-fold error": np.mean(cv_pred != sb),
                 "training error": 1 - m_.score(Zb, sb), "test error": 1 - m_.score(Zb_te, sb_te)})
svm_path = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(svm_path.to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
print("LOO error <= SV fraction for every C:", bool((svm_path["LOO error"] <= svm_path["SV fraction (LOO bound)"] + 1e-12).all()))

cv_err = svm_path["10-fold error"].to_numpy()
i_cv = int(np.argmin(cv_err))
se = np.sqrt(cv_err[i_cv] * (1 - cv_err[i_cv]) / n_b)                      # binomial standard error of the best CV error

for name, i in [("minimum of the 10-fold error", i_cv), ("one-standard-error rule", i_1se)]:

      f"{svm_path['C'][cv_err <= cv_err[i_cv] + se].min():g} and {svm_path['C'][cv_err <= cv_err[i_cv] + se].max():g}")

one-standard-error rule: C = 0.01 (10-fold error 0.0352, 101 support vectors), test error 0.0420 = 6 errors out of 143
standard error of the best 10-fold error: 0.0080; the 10-fold error stays within one standard error for C between 0.01 and 100

Figure 8.6(a) confirms Proposition 8.8: the leave-one-out error is below the fraction of support vectors for every CCC. The bound is loose when CCC is small (at C=0.003C = 0.003C=0.003 the fraction is 35%35\%35% and the leave-one-out error 5.2%5.2\%5.2%) and tight when CCC is large (at C=100C = 100C=100: 5.6%5.6\%5.6% against 4.9%4.9\%4.9%, with 24 support vectors). At the values of CCC where the classification is best (0.03 to 0.1) the fraction of support vectors is 12%12\%12% to 17%17\%17%, four to six times the leave-one-out error, so the bound is informative about the trend (the sparser the solution, the smaller the guarantee) more than about the level. Panel (b) shows the three error estimates of the chapter on one plot. The leave-one-out, the 10-fold and the test error fall from about 6%6\%6% at C=0.001C = 0.001C=0.001 to a minimum of 2.6%2.6\%2.6% to 2.8%2.8\%2.8% (leave-one-out and 10-fold) and 2.1%2.1\%2.1% (test) at C=0.03C = 0.03C=0.03 to 0.1, and rise slowly for larger CCC (to 5%5\%5% for the leave-one-out and 7%7\%7% for the test error) while the training error falls to zero: the U-shape of Chapters 4 to 6, with a mild right branch.

The selection of CCC shows the limits of the protocol. The minimum of the 10-fold error is at C=0.03C = 0.03C=0.03 (2.8%2.8\%2.8%, standard error 0.8%0.8\%0.8%) and gives 3 errors on the test set; the one-standard-error rule of Section 5.4.1 chooses C=0.01C = 0.01C=0.01 and gives 6. But the 10-fold error stays within one standard error of its minimum for every CCC between 0.01 and 100, four orders of magnitude, so the data cannot tell these values apart, and the difference between 3 and 6 test errors is of the size of the noise (the standard error of an error rate of 3%3\%3% on 143 patients is 1.4%1.4\%1.4%). The practical consequence is the one of Section 5.4.2: a coarse logarithmic grid for CCC is enough, and one should not read much into the position of the minimum.

8.7 Using SVMs in practice¶

8.7.1 Scale the features¶

The margin is a Euclidean distance, so a feature with a large scale dominates it, exactly as for kkk-nearest neighbors (Section 4.8.2) and ridge (Section 6.3.1): the SVM is not invariant to the scaling of the features. The SVM is also an optimization problem whose conditioning depends on the scales (Section 7.4). The cell compares the same linear SVM, with C=1C = 1C=1, on the raw Breast Cancer features and on the standardized ones (the standardization inside a pipeline, fitted on the training set only), by the number of solver iterations, the test accuracy and the AUC.

rows = []
for name, est in [("raw features", make_pipeline(SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0, tol=1e-4, cache_size=500))),
                  ("standardized", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0, tol=1e-4, cache_size=500)))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    est.fit(Xb_tr, sb)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    svc_ = est[-1]
    score_te = est.decision_function(Xb_te)
    rows.append({"features": name, "solver iterations": int(np.ravel(svc_.n_iter_)[0]), "support vectors": len(svc_.support_),
                 "test accuracy": np.mean(np.sign(score_te) == sb_te), "test AUC": roc_auc_score(sb_te, score_te)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
    features  solver iterations  support vectors  test accuracy  test AUC
raw features          159687807               43         0.9371    0.9937
standardized               2973               36         0.9580    0.9929

Without standardization the solver of libsvm needs about 1.6⋅1081.6\cdot 10^81.6⋅108 iterations at C=1C = 1C=1, against about 3.0⋅1033.0\cdot 10^33.0⋅103 with standardization, more than four orders of magnitude fewer. The standard deviations of the raw features range from 0.003 (the error of the fractal dimension) to 569 (the worst area), the Gram matrix is dominated by the features of large scale, and the dual problem is badly conditioned, the cause that Section 7.4 identified for gradient descent. The classifier changes too: 43 support vectors against 36 and a test accuracy of 0.937 against 0.958 (9 errors against 6). The AUC is not lower for the raw features (0.994 against 0.993), which suggests that what changes is mainly the position of the boundary and not the ordering of the patients; with 143 test patients we do not read more than that into it. The rule is the one of Chapters 2 and 4: standardize inside the pipeline, always, before an SVM.

8.7.2 SVM and logistic regression, compared with the protocols of Chapter 5¶

How does the SVM compare with the regularized logistic regression of Chapter 6? We tune CCC for both by the 10-fold cross-validation error on the same folds (the same standardized training set as above), evaluate on the test set once, and compare the two sets of predictions with McNemar’s exact test (Section 5.5.1).

rows, preds = [], {}
for name, make in [("SVM (linear)", lambda C: SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-6)),
                   ("logistic regression", lambda C: LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=10_000))]:
    errs = [np.mean(cross_val_predict(make(C), Zb, sb, cv=skf10) != sb) for C in C_grid]
    C_best = C_grid[int(np.argmin(errs))]
    fit_ = make(C_best).fit(Zb, sb)
    score_ = fit_.decision_function(Zb_te)
    preds[name] = np.sign(score_)
    rows.append({"model": name, "C chosen by 10-fold CV": C_best, "10-fold error": min(errs), "test accuracy": np.mean(preds[name] == sb_te),
                 "test errors": int(np.sum(preds[name] != sb_te)), "test AUC": roc_auc_score(sb_te, score_)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
a_, b_ = preds["SVM (linear)"], preds["logistic regression"]
n_sv_only, n_lr_only = int(np.sum((a_ == sb_te) & (b_ != sb_te))), int(np.sum((a_ != sb_te) & (b_ == sb_te)))
p_mc = binomtest(min(n_sv_only, n_lr_only), n_sv_only + n_lr_only, 0.5).pvalue if n_sv_only + n_lr_only > 0 else 1.0
print(f"patients classified correctly by the SVM only: {n_sv_only}; by the logistic regression only: {n_lr_only}; McNemar exact p-value = {p_mc:.3f}")
              model  C chosen by 10-fold CV  10-fold error  test accuracy  test errors  test AUC
       SVM (linear)                  0.0300         0.0282         0.9790            3    0.9977
logistic regression                  1.0000         0.0211         0.9650            5    0.9962
patients classified correctly by the SVM only: 2; by the logistic regression only: 0; McNemar exact p-value = 0.500

Tuned on the same folds, the SVM chooses C=0.03C = 0.03C=0.03 (10-fold error 2.8%2.8\%2.8%) and the logistic regression C=1C = 1C=1 (2.1%2.1\%2.1%): the logistic regression is ahead in cross-validation and the SVM on the test set (3 errors against 5; AUC 0.998 against 0.996). Neither lead means anything. On the 143 test patients the SVM is right and the logistic regression wrong for 2 patients, and the opposite happens for none (McNemar’s exact p=0.50p = 0.50p=0.50); the cross-validation difference of 0.7 points is smaller than the standard error of each estimate (0.8 points). Both models are linear classifiers with an ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty that differ only by the loss (Section 8.4), and on these data there is no evidence in favor of either. The choice is made on other grounds: probabilities and a smooth path in CCC for the logistic regression; sparsity in the examples, the leave-one-out bound and kernels (Chapter 9) for the SVM.

8.7.3 From scores to probabilities: Platt scaling¶

The score f(x)f(\mathbf{x})f(x) of an SVM is not a probability (Proposition 8.5), but a monotone transformation of it can be one. Platt scaling (Platt, 1999) fits the two-parameter model P(y=1∣f)=σ(Af+B)\mathbb{P}(y = 1\mid f) = \sigma(Af + B)P(y=1∣f)=σ(Af+B) by maximum likelihood, which is a logistic regression on the one-dimensional score, using held-out scores so that the fit is not distorted by the training examples (whose scores are pushed beyond the margin). It does not change the ranking of the examples: the AUC is unchanged. This is the recalibration of Section 5.6.4, and CalibratedClassifierCV(method="sigmoid") does it with cross-validation. The cell compares, for two values of CCC, the log-loss and Brier score of three probability estimates on the test set: the raw sigmoid σ(f)\sigma(f)σ(f) (which has no justification), the Platt-scaled SVM, and the logistic regression with the same CCC.

rows, slopes = [], {}
for C in [0.03, 1.0]:
    svc_ = SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-6).fit(Zb, sb)
    d_te = svc_.decision_function(Zb_te)
    p_raw = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-d_te))
    platt = CalibratedClassifierCV(SVC(kernel="linear", C=C, tol=1e-6), method="sigmoid", cv=5).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
    p_platt = platt.predict_proba(Zb_te)[:, 1]
    slopes[C] = np.mean([-cc.calibrators[0].a_ for cc in platt.calibrated_classifiers_])      # the slope A of sigma(A f + B), averaged over the 5 folds
    lr_ = LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=10_000).fit(Zb, yb_tr)
    p_lr = lr_.predict_proba(Zb_te)[:, 1]
    for name, p in [("raw sigmoid of the score", p_raw), ("Platt scaling", p_platt), ("logistic regression", p_lr)]:
        rows.append({"C": C, "probability estimate": name, "log-loss": log_loss(yb_te, p), "Brier score": brier_score_loss(yb_te, p),
                     "AUC": roc_auc_score(yb_te, d_te if name != "logistic regression" else lr_.decision_function(Zb_te))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
print("average slope A of the Platt sigmoid:", {C: round(float(a), 2) for C, a in slopes.items()})
     C     probability estimate  log-loss  Brier score    AUC
0.0300 raw sigmoid of the score    0.1667       0.0377 0.9977
0.0300            Platt scaling    0.1026       0.0247 0.9977
0.0300      logistic regression    0.1212       0.0289 0.9985
1.0000 raw sigmoid of the score    0.1201       0.0324 0.9929
1.0000            Platt scaling    0.1304       0.0350 0.9929
1.0000      logistic regression    0.0776       0.0224 0.9962
average slope A of the Platt sigmoid: {0.03: 1.74, 1.0: 0.86}

For C=0.03C = 0.03C=0.03 (the value chosen by cross-validation) the raw sigmoid of the score has a log-loss of 0.167 and a Brier score of 0.0377; Platt scaling lowers them to 0.103 and 0.0247, better than the logistic regression with the same CCC (0.121 and 0.0289). The slope of the fitted sigmoid is A≈1.7A\approx 1.7A≈1.7: with this CCC the scores are on too small a scale and the raw sigmoid is under-confident, and the calibration stretches them. For C=1C = 1C=1 the scores are on a larger scale, the slope is A≈0.9A\approx 0.9A≈0.9, and the raw sigmoid is already nearly right: Platt scaling does not help (log-loss 0.130 against 0.120, Brier 0.0350 against 0.0324), and the logistic regression is clearly better (0.078 and 0.0224, the value of Section 6.8). The AUC is the same for the raw and the Platt-scaled score, since the transformation is monotone. The lesson is that the calibration of a raw SVM score depends on CCC, through the scale of w\mathbf{w}w, and that when probabilities are needed one should either calibrate on held-out scores or use a model whose loss is a likelihood. With 143 test patients, differences of 0.01 in log-loss are within the noise: a handful of confident errors dominate this metric (Section 5.6.4).

8.7.4 More than two classes¶

The SVM is a binary classifier, and two reductions extend it to KKK classes. One-vs-rest (OvR) trains KKK classifiers, each separating one class from all the others, and predicts the class with the largest score. One-vs-one (OvO) trains K(K−1)/2K(K - 1)/2K(K−1)/2 classifiers, each on the examples of two classes only, and predicts by majority vote. For Digits (K=10K = 10K=10) these are 10 and 45 problems; the OvO problems are smaller (each uses about 2/K2/K2/K of the data). SVC always uses one-vs-one internally (its option decision_function_shape only reshapes the output), and LinearSVC uses one-vs-rest. We compare, with CCC tuned by 5-fold cross-validation on the training set (the split of Chapters 6 and 7: 1347 training and 450 test images), both reductions with the softmax regression of Section 6.6.

dg = load_digits()
Xg_tr, Xg_te, yg_tr, yg_te = train_test_split(dg.data, dg.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=dg.target)
skf5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
candidates = {
    "SVM one-vs-one (45 problems)": (make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", tol=1e-4)), {"svc__C": np.logspace(-4, 2, 7)}),
    "SVM one-vs-rest (10 problems)": (make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), OneVsRestClassifier(SVC(kernel="linear", tol=1e-4))),
                                      {"onevsrestclassifier__estimator__C": np.logspace(-4, 2, 7)}),
    "softmax regression (1 problem)": (make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=20_000)), {"logisticregression__C": np.logspace(-3, 2, 6)}),
}
rows, preds_g = [], {}
for name, (est, grid_) in candidates.items():
    search = GridSearchCV(est, grid_, cv=skf5, scoring="accuracy").fit(Xg_tr, yg_tr)
    preds_g[name] = search.predict(Xg_te)
    rows.append({"method": name, "C chosen": list(search.best_params_.values())[0], "5-fold accuracy": search.best_score_,
                 "test accuracy": np.mean(preds_g[name] == yg_te), "test errors": int(np.sum(preds_g[name] != yg_te))})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
names_g = list(preds_g)
for i in range(len(names_g)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(names_g)):
        a_, b_ = preds_g[names_g[i]] == yg_te, preds_g[names_g[j]] == yg_te
        only_a, only_b = int(np.sum(a_ & ~b_)), int(np.sum(~a_ & b_))
        p_ = binomtest(min(only_a, only_b), only_a + only_b, 0.5).pvalue if only_a + only_b else 1.0
        print(f"McNemar, {names_g[i]} vs {names_g[j]}: {only_a} vs {only_b} discordant, p = {p_:.3f}")
                        method  C chosen  5-fold accuracy  test accuracy  test errors
  SVM one-vs-one (45 problems)    1.0000           0.9799         0.9800            9
 SVM one-vs-rest (10 problems)    0.1000           0.9555         0.9556           20
softmax regression (1 problem)   10.0000           0.9673         0.9644           16
McNemar, SVM one-vs-one (45 problems) vs SVM one-vs-rest (10 problems): 15 vs 4 discordant, p = 0.019
McNemar, SVM one-vs-one (45 problems) vs softmax regression (1 problem): 10 vs 3 discordant, p = 0.092
McNemar, SVM one-vs-rest (10 problems) vs softmax regression (1 problem): 6 vs 10 discordant, p = 0.454

One-vs-one is the best of the three on this problem: 9 errors among 450 test images (0.980), against 20 (0.956) for one-vs-rest and 16 (0.964) for the softmax regression tuned in the same way (Section 6.6 reported 0.973, with CCC chosen by the log-loss: 12 errors; the choice of the criterion alone moves the result by a few images). McNemar’s test separates one-vs-one from one-vs-rest (15 against 4 discordant images, p=0.019p = 0.019p=0.019; with a Bonferroni correction for three comparisons, 0.057), and does not separate it from the softmax regression (10 against 3, p=0.092p = 0.092p=0.092) nor one-vs-rest from the softmax regression (p=0.45p = 0.45p=0.45). So the evidence favors one-vs-one over one-vs-rest, and is only suggestive against the softmax regression. A plausible reason for the first difference, which we have not tested, is that each pairwise problem (two digits) is much easier, and closer to linearly separable, than one digit against nine heterogeneous others; the price is 45 problems instead of 10, each on about a fifth of the data.

8.8 Beyond the linear SVM¶

8.8.1 The dual only needs inner products: a preview of kernels¶

Look again at the dual problem of Theorem 8.4 and at the classifier: the training data enter only through the inner products xi⊤xj\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jxi⊤​xj​ (the Gram matrix of the SMO of Section 8.5.2), and a new point enters only through xi⊤x\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}xi⊤​x:

f^(x)=∑i=1nα^iyi xi⊤x+b^.\hat f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{i=1}^n\hat\alpha_iy_i\,\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x} + \hat b .f^​(x)=i=1∑n​α^i​yi​xi⊤​x+b^.
(20)

Suppose that we first map the data with a function ϕ:Rd→Rp\boldsymbol\phi:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}^pϕ:Rd→Rp into a space of features where a linear classifier is more powerful, as in Section 6.7, and train the SVM on ϕ(xi)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}_i)ϕ(xi​). Then only the inner products k(x,z)=ϕ(x)⊤ϕ(z)k(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{z}) = \boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x})^\top\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z})k(x,z)=ϕ(x)⊤ϕ(z) are needed, and we never have to compute ϕ\boldsymbol\phiϕ if we can evaluate kkk directly. For two features and the map ϕ(x)=(x12, x22, 2x1x2, 2x1, 2x2, 1)\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x}) = (x_1^2,\ x_2^2,\ \sqrt2x_1x_2,\ \sqrt2x_1,\ \sqrt2x_2,\ 1)ϕ(x)=(x12​, x22​, 2​x1​x2​, 2​x1​, 2​x2​, 1), a direct computation gives

ϕ(x)⊤ϕ(z)=x12z12+x22z22+2x1x2z1z2+2x1z1+2x2z2+1=(x⊤z+1)2,\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{x})^\top\boldsymbol\phi(\mathbf{z}) = x_1^2z_1^2 + x_2^2z_2^2 + 2x_1x_2z_1z_2 + 2x_1z_1 + 2x_2z_2 + 1 = (\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + 1)^2 ,ϕ(x)⊤ϕ(z)=x12​z12​+x22​z22​+2x1​x2​z1​z2​+2x1​z1​+2x2​z2​+1=(x⊤z+1)2,
(21)

the polynomial kernel of degree 2: its cost is that of an inner product in R2\mathbb{R}^2R2, not in R6\mathbb{R}^6R6, and for d=30d = 30d=30 features and degree 5 the space of features has dimension (355)=324,632\binom{35}{5} = 324{,}632(535​)=324,632 while the kernel is still O(d)O(d)O(d). Chapter 9 develops the theory (which functions kkk are legitimate, the Gaussian kernel whose feature space is infinite-dimensional, the representer theorem). Here we only verify the identity on real data, and see what it buys. The features are the mean radius and mean texture of the Breast Cancer patients (standardized), the two features of Section 6.7. The first cell trains an SVM with the kernel poly (γ=1\gamma = 1γ=1, coefficient 1, degree 2) and a linear SVM on the six explicit features, and compares their decision functions.

two = ["mean radius", "mean texture"]
Xk = bc.data[two].to_numpy()
Xk_tr, Xk_te, _, _ = train_test_split(Xk, yb, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED, stratify=yb)     # the same patients as before
scaler_k = StandardScaler().fit(Xk_tr)
Zk, Zk_te = scaler_k.transform(Xk_tr), scaler_k.transform(Xk_te)


def phi2(X):
    x1, x2, r = X[:, 0], X[:, 1], np.sqrt(2)
    return np.c_[x1**2, x2**2, r * x1 * x2, r * x1, r * x2, np.ones(len(X))]


with_kernel = SVC(kernel="poly", degree=2, gamma=1, coef0=1, C=1, tol=1e-10).fit(Zk, sb)
with_features = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1, tol=1e-10).fit(phi2(Zk), sb)
d_kernel, d_features = with_kernel.decision_function(Zk_te), with_features.decision_function(phi2(Zk_te))
print(f"kernel (x.z + 1)^2 against a linear SVM on 6 explicit features: same support vectors: {set(with_kernel.support_) == set(with_features.support_)} "
      f"({len(with_kernel.support_)}); largest difference between the test decision functions: {np.abs(d_kernel - d_features).max():.1e}")
w_feat = with_kernel.dual_coef_.ravel() @ phi2(Zk)[with_kernel.support_]                         # w in the feature space, from the dual
print("weights of the six features, from the dual:", w_feat.round(3), "(the constant feature gets weight sum alpha_i y_i = 0)")

rows = []
for degree in [1, 2, 3, 5]:
    m_ = SVC(kernel="poly", degree=degree, gamma=1, coef0=1, C=1, tol=1e-8).fit(Zk, sb)
    rows.append({"degree": degree, "support vectors": len(m_.support_), "training accuracy": m_.score(Zk, sb), "test accuracy": m_.score(Zk_te, sb_te)})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))
kernel (x.z + 1)^2 against a linear SVM on 6 explicit features: same support vectors: True (106); largest difference between the test decision functions: 1.1e-10
weights of the six features, from the dual: [ 0.955 -0.28   0.467  1.655  0.55   0.   ] (the constant feature gets weight sum alpha_i y_i = 0)
 degree  support vectors  training accuracy  test accuracy
      1              119             0.8897         0.8811
      2              106             0.8991         0.8881
      3              101             0.9014         0.9091
      5              101             0.9108         0.9091

# Figure 8.7 — the same SVM with polynomial kernels of degree 1, 2 and 3 (two Breast Cancer features)
def figure_8_7():
    gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2.6, 4.2, 220), np.linspace(-2.8, 4.4, 220))
    grid_pts = np.c_[gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11.6, 3.9), sharex=True, sharey=True)
    for ax, degree in zip(axes, [1, 2, 3]):
        m_ = SVC(kernel="poly", degree=degree, gamma=1, coef0=1, C=1, tol=1e-8).fit(Zk, sb)
        d_ = m_.decision_function(grid_pts).reshape(gx.shape)
        ax.contourf(gx, gy, d_, levels=[-100, 0, 100], colors=[VERMILION, BLUE], alpha=0.10)
        ax.contour(gx, gy, d_, levels=[-1, 0, 1], colors="k", linestyles=["--", "-", "--"], linewidths=[1.0, 2.0, 1.0])
        ax.scatter(*Zk[sb == -1].T, s=14, color=VERMILION, marker="s", alpha=0.7, label="benign")
        ax.scatter(*Zk[sb == 1].T, s=14, color=BLUE, marker="o", alpha=0.7, label="malignant")
        ax.set(xlim=(-2.6, 4.2), ylim=(-2.8, 4.4), xlabel="mean radius (standardized)",
               title=f"degree {degree}: test accuracy {m_.score(Zk_te, sb_te):.3f}")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("mean texture (standardized)")
    axes[0].legend(frameon=False, loc="lower right", fontsize=9)
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_7()

The SVM with the kernel (x⊤z+1)2(\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + 1)^2(x⊤z+1)2 and the linear SVM on the six explicit features have the same 106 support vectors, and their decision functions differ by 10-10 on the test set: the kernel computes exactly the inner products of the feature space without ever forming it. The weights of the six features, recovered from the dual, show that the constant feature has weight 0 (=∑iαiyi=\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=∑i​αi​yi​, zero by the dual constraint), so the intercept is not counted twice. Higher degrees give more flexible boundaries (Figure 8.7: curved, and with wiggles near the edges of the plot, where there are no data and the polynomial extrapolates freely), but on these two features the gain in accuracy is small: the test accuracy goes from 0.881 for the linear classifier to 0.888, 0.909 and 0.909 for degrees 2, 3 and 5, that is, from 17 to 13 errors among 143 patients, a difference that the test set cannot confirm. Section 6.7 found the same for the polynomial logistic regression on these two features: a modest gain and a risk of overfitting. The conclusion is not that kernels are useless but that two features contain limited information; Chapter 9 will use richer kernels.

8.8.2 Support vector regression¶

The same ideas apply to regression. Replace the squared loss of Chapter 6 by the ε\varepsilonε-insensitive loss ℓε(r)=max⁡{0, ∣r∣−ε}\ell_\varepsilon(r) = \max\{0,\ \lvert r\rvert - \varepsilon\}ℓε​(r)=max{0, ∣r∣−ε} of the residual r=y−f(x)r = y - f(\mathbf{x})r=y−f(x): a residual smaller than ε\varepsilonε costs nothing. Support vector regression (SVR) minimizes

12∥w∥2+C∑i=1nmax⁡{0, ∣yi−w⊤xi−b∣−ε},\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^n\max\big\{0,\ \lvert y_i - \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i - b\rvert - \varepsilon\big\},21​∥w∥2+Ci=1∑n​max{0, ∣yi​−w⊤xi​−b∣−ε},
(22)

with the same CCC and the same regularization as the classifier. The derivation of the dual repeats the proof of Theorem 8.4, with two multipliers per example, αi\alpha_iαi​ for the constraint yi−f(xi)≤ε+ξiy_i - f(\mathbf{x}_i)\le\varepsilon + \xi_iyi​−f(xi​)≤ε+ξi​ and αi∗\alpha_i^\astαi∗​ for f(xi)−yi≤ε+ξi∗f(\mathbf{x}_i) - y_i\le\varepsilon + \xi_i^\astf(xi​)−yi​≤ε+ξi∗​: one finds w=∑i(αi−αi∗)xi\mathbf{w} = \sum_i(\alpha_i - \alpha_i^\ast)\mathbf{x}_iw=∑i​(αi​−αi∗​)xi​, ∑i(αi−αi∗)=0\sum_i(\alpha_i - \alpha_i^\ast) = 0∑i​(αi​−αi∗​)=0 and 0≤αi,αi∗≤C0\le\alpha_i, \alpha_i^\ast\le C0≤αi​,αi∗​≤C; the details follow the proof of Theorem 8.4 line by line. By the same argument as for the classifier, the examples inside the tube of half-width ε\varepsilonε around the fitted function have αi=αi∗=0\alpha_i = \alpha_i^\ast = 0αi​=αi∗​=0 and are not support vectors: ε\varepsilonε controls the sparsity, as CCC controls the margin violations. The cell fits SVR on the Diabetes data of Chapters 6 and 7 (the same 331/111 split; standardized features), choosing CCC by 5-fold cross-validation for each ε\varepsilonε, and compares with least squares and ridge regression.

diab_s = load_diabetes()
Xd_tr, Xd_te, yd_tr, yd_te = train_test_split(diab_s.data, diab_s.target, test_size=0.25, random_state=SEED)
kf5 = KFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)


def rmse(model, X, y):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean((model.predict(X) - y) ** 2)))


rows = [{"model": "predict the training mean", "C": np.nan, "5-fold RMSE": np.nan, "test RMSE": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((yd_tr.mean() - yd_te) ** 2))), "support vectors": np.nan}]
ols_d = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()).fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
rows.append({"model": "least squares", "C": np.nan, "5-fold RMSE": np.nan, "test RMSE": rmse(ols_d, Xd_te, yd_te), "support vectors": np.nan})
ridge_d = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), Ridge()), {"ridge__alpha": np.logspace(-2, 3, 11)}, cv=kf5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
rows.append({"model": "ridge (lambda by 5-fold CV)", "C": np.nan, "5-fold RMSE": -ridge_d.best_score_, "test RMSE": rmse(ridge_d, Xd_te, yd_te), "support vectors": np.nan})
svr_models = {}
for eps in [0, 10, 30, 50, 100]:
    gs = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVR(kernel="linear", epsilon=eps, tol=1e-4)), {"svr__C": np.logspace(-1, 2, 7)},
                      cv=kf5, scoring="neg_root_mean_squared_error").fit(Xd_tr, yd_tr)
    svr_models[eps] = gs.best_estimator_
    rows.append({"model": f"SVR, epsilon = {eps}", "C": gs.best_params_["svr__C"], "5-fold RMSE": -gs.best_score_, "test RMSE": rmse(gs, Xd_te, yd_te),
                 "support vectors": len(gs.best_estimator_[-1].support_)})
print(f"{len(yd_tr)} training patients; the standard deviation of the target is {yd_tr.std():.1f}")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False, float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.2f}"))

ridge (lambda by 5-fold CV)    NaN        56.07      53.32              NaN

# Figure 8.8 — support vector regression on one feature of Diabetes: the epsilon-tube
def figure_8_8():
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10.6, 4.2))
    j = list(diab_s.feature_names).index("bmi")
    xb_tr = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xd_tr[:, [j]])
    ax = axes[0]
    eps = 50
    m_ = SVR(kernel="linear", C=10, epsilon=eps, tol=1e-4).fit(xb_tr, yd_tr)
    grid_x = np.linspace(xb_tr.min() - 0.1, xb_tr.max() + 0.1, 100)[:, None]
    fit_ = m_.predict(grid_x)
    inside = np.abs(yd_tr - m_.predict(xb_tr)) < eps - 1e-6
    ax.scatter(xb_tr[inside], yd_tr[inside], s=14, color=SKY, alpha=0.8, label="inside the tube")
    ax.scatter(xb_tr[~inside], yd_tr[~inside], s=18, color=VERMILION, marker="^", alpha=0.9, label="support vectors")
    ax.plot(grid_x, fit_, color="k", lw=2, label="SVR fit")
    ax.plot(grid_x, fit_ + eps, color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--", label=r"$\pm\varepsilon$ tube")
    ax.plot(grid_x, fit_ - eps, color="k", lw=1.0, ls="--")
    ax.set(xlabel="body mass index (standardized)", ylabel="disease progression", title=f"(a) $\\varepsilon = {eps}$: {int((~inside).sum())} of {len(yd_tr)} are support vectors")
    ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="upper left")
    ax = axes[1]
    eps_values = [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100, 120]
    n_sv = [len(SVR(kernel="linear", C=10, epsilon=e, tol=1e-4).fit(xb_tr, yd_tr).support_) for e in eps_values]
    ax.plot(eps_values, n_sv, color=BLUE, lw=2, marker="o", ms=5)
    ax.set(xlabel=r"half-width of the tube $\varepsilon$", ylabel="number of support vectors", title="(b) $\\varepsilon$ controls the sparsity")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()


figure_8_8()

The test RMSE of least squares (53.37), ridge (53.32) and SVR (53.0 to 54.6 according to ε\varepsilonε) differ by less than two points, and the cross-validation RMSE of all of them is between 56.0 and 56.6: on 111 test patients these differences are not resolved (the standard deviation of the target is 77.7 and the RMSE of the baseline 74.9). The ε\varepsilonε-insensitive loss does not improve on the squared loss here, which is the likelihood-based choice when the noise is roughly Gaussian; its advantage would show with heavy-tailed noise, which we have not tested. What ε\varepsilonε buys is sparsity: all 331 patients are support vectors for ε=0\varepsilon = 0ε=0 (where the loss is the absolute error ∣r∣\lvert r\rvert∣r∣), 138 for ε=50\varepsilon = 50ε=50 and only 25 for ε=100\varepsilon = 100ε=100 (more than a standard deviation of the target), at a cost of 0.8 points of RMSE with respect to least squares. Figure 8.8(a) shows the tube for the body mass index alone (161 of the 331 patients are on or outside the tube of half-width 50, with C=10C = 10C=10) and panel (b) the number of support vectors falling from 331 to 15 as ε\varepsilonε goes from 0 to 120.

8.9 Summary¶

  • Geometry. The distance from x\mathbf{x}x to the hyperplane w⊤x+b=0\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b = 0w⊤x+b=0 is ∣w⊤x+b∣/∥w∥\lvert\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\rvert/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∣w⊤x+b∣/∥w∥ (Proposition 8.1). Among the hyperplanes that separate the data, the hard-margin SVM chooses the one with the largest margin by minimizing 12∥w∥2\tfrac12\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^221​∥w∥2 subject to yi(w⊤xi+b)≥1y_i(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}_i + b)\ge 1yi​(w⊤xi​+b)≥1; the margin is 1/∥w∥1/\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert1/∥w∥. In Worked example 8.1 the solution is w=(0,1)\mathbf{w} = (0, 1)w=(0,1), b=−1b = -1b=−1, with three support vectors.

  • Duality (Theorems 8.2 and 8.4). The dual maximizes ∑iαi−12∑i,jαiαjyiyjxi⊤xj\sum_i\alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_j∑i​αi​−21​∑i,j​αi​αj​yi​yj​xi⊤​xj​ with ∑iαiyi=0\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0∑i​αi​yi​=0 and αi≥0\alpha_i\ge 0αi​≥0 (and αi≤C\alpha_i\le Cαi​≤C for the soft margin). Then w=∑iαiyixi\mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw=∑i​αi​yi​xi​ and complementary slackness makes the solution sparse: only the support vectors (αi>0\alpha_i > 0αi​>0) matter, and ∥w∥2=∑iαi\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 = \sum_i\alpha_i∥w∥2=∑i​αi​ in the hard-margin case. On Iris (setosa/versicolor) two flowers out of 100 determine the classifier, and on the Breast Cancer training set 36 patients out of 426 do (C=1C = 1C=1).

  • Soft margin and the hinge loss (Proposition 8.3). With slacks, the SVM minimizes 1n∑imax⁡{0,1−mi}+λ2∥w∥2\frac1n\sum_i\max\{0, 1 - m_i\} + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2n1​∑i​max{0,1−mi​}+2λ​∥w∥2 with λ=1/(Cn)\lambda = 1/(Cn)λ=1/(Cn): a regularized linear classifier like the logistic regression of Chapter 6, with the hinge loss in place of the log-loss. The examples are of three kinds: beyond the margin (αi=0\alpha_i = 0αi​=0; 390 of 426 at C=1C = 1C=1), on it (0<αi<C0 < \alpha_i < C0<αi​<C; 20) and inside it or misclassified (αi=C\alpha_i = Cαi​=C; 16). For a separable data set every C≥C0C\ge C_0C≥C0​ (the largest hard-margin multiplier; C0=125C_0 = 125C0​=125 on Breast Cancer) gives the hard-margin classifier exactly.

  • What the hinge loss estimates (Proposition 8.5). Its population minimizer is sign⁡(2η−1)\operatorname{sign}(2\eta - 1)sign(2η−1), the Bayes classifier, and not η\etaη: the score is a distance, not a probability. Logistic regression has the same representation w=∑iαiyixi\mathbf{w} = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\mathbf{x}_iw=∑i​αi​yi​xi​ with αi=Cσ(−mi)\alpha_i = C\sigma(-m_i)αi​=Cσ(−mi​), never exactly zero: the hinge loss hardens the sigmoid into a step. Probabilities for an SVM come from Platt scaling, which helps or not depending on CCC (log-loss 0.167→0.1030.167\to 0.1030.167→0.103 at C=0.03C = 0.03C=0.03, 0.120→0.1300.120\to 0.1300.120→0.130 at C=1C = 1C=1).

  • Algorithms (Section 8.5). The subgradient method with the step 1/(λk)1/(\lambda k)1/(λk) has the guarantee G2(1+ln⁡K)/(2λK)G^2(1 + \ln K)/(2\lambda K)G2(1+lnK)/(2λK) for the average iterate (Theorem 8.6; loose by three to four orders of magnitude on Breast Cancer, whose measured gaps decay like 1/k1/k1/k), SMO updates two multipliers at a time with a closed-form step (Proposition 8.7; 20,89920{,}89920,899 iterations at C=1C = 1C=1, against 9,5249{,}5249,524 for libsvm’s second-order choice of the pair), and dual coordinate descent solves the problem with the intercept in the weights. SVC (libsvm), LinearSVC (liblinear) and SGDClassifier solve slightly different problems because of the treatment of the intercept.

  • Generalization (Section 8.6). The margin bound of Theorem 3.7 is vacuous on Breast Cancer with the worst-case radius (1.7 or more) and below 1 with the root-mean-square radius only for C≤0.1C\le 0.1C≤0.1, but it correctly ranks the hard margin last: its capacity term, proportional to ∥w∥\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert∥w∥, is the largest (28.4) and its test error the highest (7.0%7.0\%7.0%). The leave-one-out error is bounded by the fraction of support vectors (Proposition 8.8), verified for eleven values of CCC (bound loose when CCC is small, tight when it is large). Cross-validation cannot tell apart the values of CCC between 0.01 and 100: a coarse logarithmic grid is enough.

  • Practice (Section 8.7). Standardize inside a pipeline: without it the libsvm solver needed 1.6⋅1081.6\cdot 10^81.6⋅108 iterations instead of 3⋅1033\cdot 10^33⋅103. On Breast Cancer the tuned SVM and the tuned logistic regression are statistically indistinguishable (3 against 5 test errors, McNemar p=0.50p = 0.50p=0.50). On Digits one-vs-one (9 errors out of 450) beats one-vs-rest (20; McNemar p=0.019p = 0.019p=0.019) and is suggestively better than the softmax regression (16; p=0.092p = 0.092p=0.092).

  • Beyond linear. The dual uses only inner products, so xi⊤xj\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jxi⊤​xj​ can be replaced by a kernel k(xi,xj)k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)k(xi​,xj​): for k=(x⊤z+1)2k = (\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{z} + 1)^2k=(x⊤z+1)2 the kernel SVM and the linear SVM on the six explicit features have the same decision function (difference ∼10−10\sim 10^{-10}∼10−10). On two Breast Cancer features the gain of a higher degree is small. Support vector regression minimizes the ε\varepsilonε-insensitive loss; on Diabetes it does not beat least squares (test RMSE 53.0 to 54.6 against 53.4), but ε\varepsilonε makes the solution sparse (25 support vectors out of 331 for ε=100\varepsilon = 100ε=100).

Data sources¶

  • Iris: R. A. Fisher, “The use of multiple measurements in taxonomic problems”, Annals of Eugenics 7(2), 179–188 (1936). Bundled with scikit-learn; Figures 8.1 and 8.2 use the petal length and width.

  • Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic): W. N. Street, W. H. Wolberg and O. L. Mangasarian, “Nuclear feature extraction for breast tumor diagnosis”, IS&T/SPIE 1993 International Symposium on Electronic Imaging: Science and Technology, volume 1905, 861–870 (1993). Bundled with scikit-learn. The target is recoded so that malignant =+1= +1=+1; the training and test sets are the stratified split of Chapters 6 and 7.

  • Digits: E. Alpaydin and C. Kaynak, “Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits”, UCI Machine Learning Repository (1998). The test portion of the data set, 1,797 images of 8×88\times 88×8 pixels, is bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Diabetes: B. Efron, T. Hastie, I. Johnstone and R. Tibshirani, “Least Angle Regression”, Annals of Statistics 32(2), 407–499 (2004). Bundled with scikit-learn.

  • Constructed data (flagged in the text): the five points of Worked example 8.1 and the small data sets of Exercises 8.1, 8.2 and 8.5, chosen so that the solution can be found by hand. All the experiments of the chapter use the real data sets above.

  • V. N. Vapnik, Statistical Learning Theory, Wiley, 1998. The theory behind the margin and the leave-one-out bound; see also V. Vapnik and O. Chapelle, “Bounds on error expectation for support vector machines”, Neural Computation 12(9), 2013–2036 (2000).

  • C. J. C. Burges, “A tutorial on support vector machines for pattern recognition”, Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 2(2), 121–167 (1998). A short and clear introduction with the geometry of Section 8.2.

The reference books; the second connects SVMs with regularization and with the loss functions of Section 8.4.

  • S. Boyd and L. Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization, Cambridge University Press, 2004, Chapter 5. Lagrange duality and the KKT conditions used in Theorems 8.2 and 8.4.

McAuliffe, “Convexity, classification, and risk bounds”, Journal of the American Statistical Association 101(473), 138–156 (2006). Why minimizing the hinge loss leads to the Bayes classifier (Proposition 8.5).

8.10 Exercises¶

Difficulty: ★ warm-up, ★★ core, ★★★ challenge. Try each exercise before reading the hint; solutions and detailed outlines are in Appendix C.

Manual (analytical) exercises¶

Exercise 8.1 ★ — A hard-margin SVM by hand. The negative points are x1=(0,0)\mathbf{x}_1 = (0, 0)x1​=(0,0), x2=(1,1)\mathbf{x}_2 = (1, 1)x2​=(1,1) and the positive points are x3=(2,0)\mathbf{x}_3 = (2, 0)x3​=(2,0), x4=(3,1)\mathbf{x}_4 = (3, 1)x4​=(3,1), x5=(4,−1)\mathbf{x}_5 = (4, -1)x5​=(4,−1). Exercise 8.4 ★★★ — From soft to hard. The data are separable, α^\hat{\boldsymbol\alpha}α^ is a solution of the hard-margin dual, and C0=max⁡iα^iC_0 = \max_i\hat\alpha_iC0​=maxi​α^i​. On the Breast Cancer data, for n∈{50,100,200,426}n\in\{50, 100, 200, 426\}n∈{50,100,200,426} draw 30 random stratified subsets of the training set, fit a linear SVM with C=0.1C = 0.1C=0.1 (on standardized features, fitted inside a pipeline on the subset), and record the fraction of support vectors, the leave-one-out error on the subset (by explicit refits) and the error on the common test set. Plot the three quantities against nnn on logarithmic axes, with the means and the standard deviations over the 30 draws. Does the fraction of support vectors decrease with nnn, and how does the test error compare with the leave-one-out error and with the bound of Proposition 8.8?

What comes next¶

We have a convex, sparse, margin-based classifier, and its dual form is made of inner products. Chapter 9 exploits this fact to the end: replacing xi⊤xj\mathbf{x}_i^\top\mathbf{x}_jxi⊤​xj​ by a kernel k(xi,xj)k(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{x}_j)k(xi​,xj​) gives nonlinear classifiers of infinite capacity that are still convex programs, and the representer theorem will show that the same reasoning applies to ridge regression (Proposition 6.12), to the logistic regression and to every penalized method of the form ∑iℓ(yi,f(xi))+λ∥f∥2\sum_i\ell(y_i, f(\mathbf{x}_i)) + \lambda\lVert f\rVert^2∑i​ℓ(yi​,f(xi​))+λ∥f∥2. The smo function of this chapter, which uses only a Gram matrix, will work with kernels without any change, and the polynomial kernel of Section 8.8.1 will be joined by the Gaussian kernel. Chapter 10 replaces the ℓ2\ell_2ℓ2​ penalty by an ℓ1\ell_1ℓ1​ penalty, which is also non-differentiable and also produces sparsity, but in the features (the coordinates of w\mathbf{w}w) and not in the examples; its algorithms, proximal gradient and coordinate descent, are close relatives of the subgradient method and of the dual coordinate descent of Section 8.5. Chapter 11 returns to nonlinear models with decision trees and ensembles, whose probabilities need the recalibration of Section 8.7.3. In Part IV the hinge loss reappears as one of the losses for training neural networks, and the questions of this chapter (what a loss estimates, how a margin controls generalization, why the optimization finds a sparse or a large-margin solution) become central.
